Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity of giving a very direct contradiction to a statement that appeared on Wednesday, January 24, in L'Evenement, a newspaper published in the city of Quebec. I would have been able to correct this sooner, had I been better acquainted with the language in which the statement was originally printed. The article begins with large headlines:
Hon. Mr. Oliver, late Liberal minister, requests immediate conscription in Canada. This Liberal leader lets the cat out of the bag. He declares that if the Liberal party came

back to power, conscription would be enforced at once. Mr. Oliver reproaches Mr. Sevigny for not preaching immediate enlistment to his
constituents during the campaign.
The article goes on:
It ill becomes Mr. Cannon to charge the Conservative Government with the intention of enforcing conscription in Canada. It is evident to those who follow the debates at Ottawa that were a Liberal administration in power conscription would come at once. Hon. Mr. Oliver, one of Sir Wilfrid's first lieutenants, let the cat out of the bag when in the warmth of his oratory he stated:
'The true policy to follow, and which the present Government should Immediately adopt, would be to enforce conscription throughout Canada. Recruiting is not satisfactory, and this expedient would settle the whole question.'
The left-
That is the Opposition.
-seemed to receive this declaration with marked satisfaction.
Further to confirm Mr. Oliver's remarks we find the following extract in the report of yesterday's sitting, which is very significant. Mr. Oliver criticises the Government for his apparent lack of organization, and the system followed in recruiting men, and declares that, in his opinion, had things been managed differently, Canada could to-day count her 500,000 men. "We must not forget,' says he, 'that more than 50,000 men who had enlisted since the beginning of the war, have been later rejected for physical unfitness. Our duty is to send to the firing line half a million men absolutely fit from a physical standpoint.' The only possible solution, according to Mr. Oliver, is the establishment of conscription in Canada. Mr. Oliver was particularly aggressive throughout his speech which can be summed up thus:	Conscription is necessary in Canada.
Mr. Oliver then alluded to the campaign now being waged in Dorchester, and made it a pretext to attack Jdr. Sevigny because he did not choose to make of his electoral campaign a recruiting tour. Here is how Mr. Sevigny addresses his constituents; said he:	'Every
one has a duty to perform in the present war. Some have enlisted to go to the firing line, but those who remain have nevertheless a very important duty to fulfil, that of providing for our agricultural needs, and other requirements.' Mr. Oliver felt indignant at such manner of speech, and claimed that Mr. Sevigny ought to have impressed upon his electors the necessity of enlisting for active service. Mr. Oliver judges that the Government has not the question of military enlistment much at heart, and reiterates his request that conscription be enforced.
I desire to say that the assertion contained in this article is absolutely untrue; and if I would be permitted, I would like to read from the speech referred to the only remarks of mine that included the word "conscription" or related in any way to that matter. It will not be very long and I wish to have the matter absolutely settled. On Tuesday, January 23, 1917, on

page 80 of the Unrevised Hansard I am quoted as saying:
Voluntary service has never had a chance in this country under the administration of our friends. For my own part I have said in this House before, and I am prepared to say it again, that in the case of such a world struggle as we are now engaged in National Service is the only logical service; National Service, I say, that will call up the manhood of the nation for military service. But it must be recognized that there are many things that are right in theory that it is not possible to put into practice. I do not challenge the Government because they have not put conscription in force, although they talked it, hinted) at it, and tried to get credit for it without doing it. The fault I have to find is that, depending on voluntary service, we never gave voluntary service a fair chance.

On the motion of the Hon. J. D. Hazen (Minister of Marine) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolutions, Mr. Blain in the Chair:
1.	That it is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council may, from time to time, advance and pay to the Corporation of the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, hereinafter called the Corporation, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of one and a half million dollars, as are required to enable the Corporation to carry on the construction of. such terminal facilities as are necessary to properly equip the port of Quebec.
2.	That during the period of construction of the terminal facilities mentioned in these Resolutions, the interest payable on the debentures receivable by the Minister of Finance in exchange for such advances, shall be deemed to be money required to construct and to be part of the cost of construction of the said terminal facilities, and such interest may be paid out of the said sum of one and a half million dollars.
3.	That the Corporation shall submit to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries for approval, monthly applications for such advances, with statements showing total expenditure on different items in detail, and upon approval, authority for the payment of the amount applied for may be granted by the Governor in Council.
4.	That the Corporation shall upon any advances being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance, debentures of the Corporation equal in par value to the advance so made, repayable within twenty-five years from the date of issue and bearing interest payable half-yearly at the rate of three and one-half per centum per annum.
5.	That the principal and interest of any sums advanced under any Act founded on these Resolutions, shall be payable by the Corporation out of all its property, assets, tools, rates, dues, penalties and other sources of revenue and income whatsoever, and shall be a charge thereon next after, and have precedence in regard to payment next after, all debentures or bonds issued J>y the Corporation-amounting-to the sum of one million one hundred and fifty thousand dollars, under Chapter forty-eight of the Statutes of 1898, Chapter thirty-four of the Statutes of 1899, and Chapter thirty-six of the Statutes of 1907.

What amount of security is already outstanding against Quebec harbour, and what is the financial standing of the corporation of the Quebec Harbour Commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The amount advanced to
the Harbour Commissioners by the Government since these works were undertaken by

authority of the Statute of 1913 is $5,500,000, and in order to complete the plans that have been approved a further expenditure of $1,500,000 is necessary. In addition, there are bonds outstanding in connection with the old scheme of haribour development there, certain of which are held by the public. In all the Acts that have been passed, provision is made that bonds issued by the old commission to private individuals, and still in private hands, shall take precedence over the advances made since 1914. As the hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) knows certain other advances were made by the Government in the old days, upon which no interest was paid. I think there is fair reason for believing, in view of the development of the harbour and the increase in the revenue, that the interest on these will be ultimately paid.

What was the
amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It was placed on Hansard when the Act of 1913 was introduced, and has been stated several times since, but I have not the information at the moment.
The Bill to be founded upon this resolution-it is practically a copy of the resolution-is in the same terms as the Acts of 1913 and 1914. Since the commencement of the harbour development under the commission, the revenues of the harbour have increased very largely. In the year 1913 the revenue from the harbour was $126,000; during the last year it was $288,000, an increase of $162,000.
What was the revenue during the intervening years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not the figures, but the revenue has increased year by year. It is expected that when this work is completed very much more business will be done than has been done in the past. That is why, even under existing conditions, we ask that the work be proceeded with so that at the earliest possible date the harbour will do the very much larger business which is expected upon the completion of the work and obtain the increased revenue which will naturally result. It is anticipated that much larger vessels will in a short time ply on the St. Lawrence river, and owing to the fact that between Montreal and Quebec there the channel is not deeper than thirty feet, vessels of more than that draught will have to make their terminus at Quebec. From the standpoint of common sense and ordinary business prudence, I think it 
would be a very great mistake not to proceed to finish this work.
What changes have been made in the personnel of the Quebec Harbour Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Of the $1,500,000, $700,000 will have to be spent during the present year. Probably it will be three years before the total amount is expended. Advances will be made from time to time, probably covering a period of three seasons. The original commission consisted of Sir William Price, chairman; Mr. Gravel, who comes from the south shore, and Mr. Letellier. Sir William Price resigned as chairman of the commission and the other commissioners forwarded their resignations at the same time. The reason given by Sir William for his resignation was that he had very extensive business affairs on his hands; in addition to that he had enlisted for overseas service and, having raised a regiment he expected to go to the front. He would not, therefore, be able to give that attention to the duties of the position which its importance demanded. A new commission was accordingly- appointed, consisting of Mr. L'Esperance, formerly member for Montmagny, Mr. Gravel, former commissioner, and Mr. Pennington, a gentleman engaged in the lumber industry in the city of Quebec.
What is Captain Murray's position?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Murray is harbour master. He was appointed by the old commission, of which Sir William Price was chairman.
I suggest that the next time this matter is taken up, a map should be placed upon the table shewing the progress of the work.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a proper suggestion; I shall be delighted to comply with it.
Is that work to be executed in the river itself, or will it be necessary to expropriate land?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand that all necessary expropriations have been made. About $127,000 worth of dredging is to be performed. An addition is to be built to the elevator, and the elevator conveyors have to be completed. The two latter items will amount, I believe, to nearly $800,000. These are the principal works to be carried on, though a further work is necessary in connection with the completion of the wharf.,
Will my hon. iriend arrange with the Minister of Railways to have wheat brought from the West to that station?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have no doubt that the harbour commissioners wall do their utmost to have wheat brought from the west to that elevator. Wheat did come to the elevator during this year. The commissioners were handicapped, I believe, by a lack of facilities for getting the wheat speedily from the elevator to the ship, a floating elevator being used for that purpose. When the conveyors are built that difficulty will be overcome. They were hampered, also, by the fact that a million bushels of grain had to remain in the elevator a considerable length of time because of difficulty in getting it out, during which time many millions of bushels could have gone through the elevator. The harbour commissioners fully believe that upon the completion of the elevator they will do a very large business in shipping grain from the port of Quebec, particularly in view of the fact that the Grand Trunk Pacific and Canadian Northern railways are now running into that city. I may mention that the revenues of the Montreal harbour commission last year were the largest in the history of the harbour. Besides paying all expenses, outstanding bills, and interest, the Montreal harbour commissioners had a surplus of something like $25,000 or $30,000. A very large grain business was done last year in the city of Montreal, and it is reasonable to expect that as the Canadian west grows and as its production of grain increases more ships will go to Montreal and Quebec. Moreover, as the hafbour facilities at these ports are perfected, there will be larger shipments from Canadian ports and not so much through American ports.

From information that I had from a colonization agent last fall, the business done by the Grand Trunk Pacific railway between Cochrane and Quebec and Amos was excellent. The road was very much encouraged by the support given to it.

I notice that the loan is secured by debentures of the corporation repayable in twenty-five years and bearing interest at 3i per cent. Does the minister -expect to secure money at that rate for these bonds, or is that the rate that is asked from other corporations of a similar nature?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It is not believed for a moment that the Government can borrow
money at 3} per cent. Authority is given to the Government by Parliament to make advances from time to time to the harbour commissioners of Montreal, and, in this case, to the harbour commissioners of Quebec, for the carrying on of work that is approved by the Governor in Council on the recommendation of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. This money the Government of Canada advances to the harbour commissioners who pay interest at the rate of 3i per cent. It is a rate which, at the time this policy was first embarked on, when financial conditions were very different from what they are at present and the country could borrow money at a rate pretty close to three and one-half per cent, involved little or no charge upon the country. Under existing conditions, of course, the country cannot borrow money at three and one-half per cent. But at the same time, in view of the fact that this is a splendid public work, that the work that is being done by the harbour commissioners at Montreal, is in the interest of the West and of every part of the country that .the very be6t facilities should be afforded for the handling of the freight and traffic of the country during the summer from the ports of Montreal and Quebec, it has not been thought desirable to increase that rate of interest. As a matter of fact, to the extent of the difference between the rate of interest paid by the commissioners and the rate paid by the Government on money it borrows, the country does assist the harbour commissioners. But it is fair to remember that in other parts of the country very large sums of money are spent for the development of the harbours by the Public Works Department upon which no interest at all is charged to ^ the local authorities. It is true that from those harbours that are under the jurisdiction of the Public Works Department certain revenues are derived in the shape of fees; but, as a rule, I do not think the revenue received at any of those harbours would, under normal conditions, pay three and one-half per cent interest on the public money that has been expended to develop them. I refer to harbours like Port Arthur, Toronto, St. John, Halifax, Victoria, Vancouver and [DOT]others.
. Mr. SINCLAIR:	The commissioners at
Quebec seem to have made a great mistake in not going to the Public Works Department instead of to my hon. friend because apparently had they done so they would have got off without paying any interest.

In looking over the Estimates I find four or five millions of dollars proposed to be voted by the Public Works Department for improvements at Toronto, Port Arthur, and other harbours; and there is no reason that I can see why Quebec should not be treated in the same way as Toronto. I think the Government ought to state what their policy is in regard to harbour improvements throughout the Dominion, and that one system should be adopted for all harbours of this kind, instead of allowing large sums to be spent on ce rtain harbours without any interest being paid, while in other cases interest is charge 1,
Resolution reported, read the first and second time and agreed to.

DISMISSAL OF COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS AT MIDDLETON, N.S.
speechtext:
For a copy of all papers, telegrams, orders in council, etc., with reference to the dismissal of Mr. Schaffner, late Collector of Customs at Middleton, N.S.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in moving this
motion I desire to say just a word or two, but I hope that I shall be able to advert to the matter later on in, the session when the papers have been brought down. The motion asks for a copy of all papers, telegrams and orders in council in reference to the dismissal of Mr. Schaffner, Collector of Customs at Middleton, in the county of Annapolis. Mr. Schaffner, I- am informed, was the Collector of Customs at the port of Middleton for a great number of years, and on the 27th December last he was dismissed under the following notice from the Commissioner of Customs:
Ottawa, December 27, 1916.
L. P. Schaffner, Esq.,
Middleton, N.S.
Sir,-I am directed to inform you that under order in council of 22nd December, 1916, you are dismissed from office as Collector of Customs of the port of Middleton, Nova Scotia, on account of political partisanship.
Under the direction of the department, Mr. Schaffner was removed from office. I am informed, whether accurately or not I cannot say, tout I believe my information to be accurate, that he .vas not a political partisan and had not been guilty of any conduct which might be strictly termed partisan for a great number of years at least. I am prepared to assume that he was guilty of no partisan act, at least since 1911, and I submit that if his head were to fall for such a reason, he should have been removed a very long while ago. Mr. Schaffner is an elderly gentleman* not enjoying good health, and his only son, I believe-I may not be correct as to that- has been fighting overseas in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, was wounded, and is at the present time in a hospital in England. The man appointed in his stead was

a young man eligible for service abroad and twenty-five years of age.
I ask the attention of the House just for a moment or two to point out one or two objections to the action of the department in dismissing Mr. Schaffner. It has been pointed out already that the present Administration occupy the Treasury Benches by grace of the Opposition, or of Parliament, and not by the consent of the people of this country. I think it is a fair statement for me to make that since October last, unless for very well founded and serious cause, the Government should have done nothing except carry on the war and such other things as were necessary in the administration of the civil affairs of this country. Whether or not Mr. Schaffner was guilty of political partisanship during the last two or three months, at least since the expiration of this present Parliament, which was, I think,on October 7, 1916, he should not have been removed from office for such a cause. The Government have given notice of their intention to apply to Parliament for an extension of the Parliamentary term. That question will come up later for consideration by Parliament, and I assume that every hon. gentleman will be prepared to deal with it upon the then existing facts. But they can hardly expect a fair and absolutely non-partisan consideration of that proposal by Parliament, or the country, if they continue carrying on a partisan government during the extended term, the term which was given them purely and solely for the purpose of carrying on affairs relating to the war. On November 27, 1915, an order in council was passed by the Government which I would like to read to the House. I have not a copy of the order, but I am reading it from a publication known as the Military Hospitals Commission Bulletin, and it is as follows:-
That in making appointments to the Government iCivil Service, preference be given to the returned members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force, especially those who through disability caused by active military service are unable to All their previous occupations; such appointments to be subject to the provision of the Civil Service Acts and to be made with due regard to the capacity of any applicant to discharge the duties of the position to which it is proposed to appoint him. I
I submit that under that order in council, if this Government deemed it proper to dismiss Mr. Schaffner, they were in honour bound to fill that position by the appointment of a returned soldier. If Mr. Schaffner had been guilty of any reprehensible conduct what could be more proper and correct than the appointment to the office of his son, who has actually served at the front, and who is to-day in hospital? Then, if that courtesy would not be extended to the dismissed official, there are, I submit, in Nova Scotia, many returned soldiers who are quite capable of filling such a position. That order in council, which I have just read to the House, I understand, was intended to apply to the inside service; at least it was subject to that narrow interpretation and in order to make sure that it applied to the outside service as well, another order in council was passed on October 12, 1916. I have not a copy of that order in council, but the publication which I am reading summarizes it in the following language:-
Both in the Inside and Outside Services preference will be given to men' who have served overseas and been honourably discharged, especially to those unable to fill their previous occupations owing to disability caused by active military service, and no examination fee will be required. During the war, no male of military age without a badge shall be appointed.
The objections which I wish to urge against the removal of Mr. Schaffner from office are, first, that he should not have been dismissed at all. I say that he was not guilty of partisan conduct. But if he was, the offence was committed many years ago, and the friends of the Administration if they wished to exercise their right to demand his dismissal on that ground, .should have done so long ago, or at all events before the expiration of the Parliamentary term on October 7, 1916. I say that the Government have no right now to exercise their power of dismissal of civil servants for an offence of political partisanship committed long before October 7, 1916. Acts of this nature are not calculated to secure, from Parliament or from the country proper and fair consideration of the proposals which the Government have presented to Parliament for the extension of the present parliamentary term., and which proposals naturally find considerable support in Canada. I say further that the Government, having decided upon the removal of Mr. Schaffner, should have observed the terms of their own order in council passed in October, 1916, to the effect that in future appointments to the Civil Service, both l'nside and Outside, preference should be given to returned soldiers.
The Government, in this case have openly disregarded their own order in council of

October, 1915, and the supple-
4 p.m. mentary order in council passed on October 12, 1916, which latter states that " during the war no male of military age without a badge shall be appointed." Surely the Government meant that this order in council should be enforced. At least, I should not like to believe that they ivere attempting to deceive the public, and had no intention of adhering to the principle laid down in their order in council. In view of all the circumstances, I submit that Mr. Schaffner should be restored to office, and the Government should not be content to rest under the imputation of having made an appointment in contravention of their own order in council. If Mr. Schaffner is not restored to office, the new appointee of the Government should be removed, and a man appointed whose qualifications come within the terms of the order in council which I have quoted.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Customs):
maintopic: DISMISSAL OF COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS AT MIDDLETON, N.S.
speechtext:
I have no objection at all to the papers being brought down. I should like to say a word on the motion. The hon. gentleman knows that there has been a standing rule for a great many years that any official who takes part in a political campaign or interferes in politics in any way shall be liable to dismissal, a statement to that effect by a member of the House of Commons to the head of the department being considered sufficient evidence on which to dismiss the official. That has been the practice not only since 1911, but during the time the hon. gentleman was sitting on this side of the House, when many dismissals took place by the Liberal Government simply on the word of the member representing the constituency concerned. In the present case, Mr. Schaffner had evidently been interfering in politics. I was so advised by the member representing that constituency, and I acted on the rule which has been followed for the last fifteen or twenty years. Personally, I dislike to dismiss an official, but at the same time I think we all agree that when a person accepts a Government position it is much better that so. long as he occupies that position he would not interfere .in politics, no matter which side he supports. This official certainly knew the rule, and that he was liable to dismissal. With reference to the young man who took the place of Mr. Schaffner, I understand that he had offered his services for overseas, but had been rejected. The statement, therefore, of
[Mr. A. K. Maclean. [
the hon. member that this man was fit for overseas service and should have gone to the front falls to the ground.
With reference to the orders in council which the hon. member has referred to, 1 believe that the Government are acting on them right up to the very letter. So far as my own department is concerned, since these orders. in council were passed, we have done everything in our power to have every vacant position filled by a returned soldier. I have done that in many cases, and am still doing so. Whenever a vacancy occurs in any constituency I make every possible effort to get a returned soldier to fill it, and if there is no returned soldier available in the locality, I get a' returned soldier from some other locality to fill the position temporarily, until a returned soldier from that particular district returns home and will accept the position.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the member making the recommendation upon which this dismissal was made, I desire to say a word or two before the resolution passes. With the manner of bringing thi3 matter before the House to-day by the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), I have no complaint to make, but I am bound to think that had the hon. gentleman been fully seized of the facts, he would not have made the speech which he did. I am also bound to think that the friends of the dismissed officer and perhaps the dismiss, ed officer himself, who exerted themselves to have the hon. gentleman bring this matter up, were not serving the best interest of that official; because it is incumbent upon me to make certain statements which I

would not have made of my own free will, but which in self defence I must refer to in public. I am free to admit that in connection with this matter I have erred, but my fault, as I see it to-day, does not lie in the fact that a few months ago I made the recommendation for the dismissal of Mr. L. P. Schaffner of Middleton, but rather in the fact that I did not make the recommendation shortly after the election in 1911, because, as my hon. friend has intimated, this Mr. Schaffner, before the Dominion election of 1911, was an exceedingly offensive, active and obnoxious partisan. He was one of the individuals who frequented every loafing place in the town attacking myself, attacking the Liberal-Conservative party and rendering himself obnoxious in every respect to the members of the Liberal-Conservative party. Of course, had I been so minded, I could, immediately after the election of 1911, have made a recommendation to the minister and procured his dismissal. I was, however, seized with compassion for the individual. While I have made some recommendations for dismissal in various parts of my constituency which I represent, Mr. Schaffner is the first resident of my own town who has lost office by' reason of the change of Government, and it was because of sympathy and not because of my expecting to gain any political advantage that he was allowed to remain in office as long as he was. I well remember meeting Mr. Schaffner on the day following the Dominion election, and I well remember the look of distress and woe upon his countenance on that occasion, a look somewhat similar to the expressions on the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite since the Dorchester election, and I was struck with pity.

maintopic: DISMISSAL OF COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS AT MIDDLETON, N.S.
speechtext: Easy. You have not heard the full story of the Dorchester election yet.

maintopic: DISMISSAL OF COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS AT MIDDLETON, N.S.
speechtext:
No, I have not heard it, but I have seen it depicted on the hon. gentleman's face. We have nothing to fear from the story of the Dorchester election. The Conservative party can hear the full report with considerably more pride and satisfaction than the Liberal party can hear it.
I told Mr. Schaffner on that occasion, being struck with sympathy, that, notwithstanding his offences in the past, he had nothing to fear; all he had to do was to go and sin no more.. But Mr. Schaffner did not see fit to do that. From that time

to the time of his dismissal he kept up the same old practice. Some time afterwards I heard of Mr. Schaffner attending a caucus of the Liberal party in the town of Middleton, a meeting at which candidates to represent the party were nominated, a meeting when work on the revision of voters' lists was done. I went to some of Mr. -Schaffner's friends after that and I asked them to point out to Mr. Schaffner that if this thing continued he could not expect to retain his position. I believe, and, in fact, I have been informed that Liberals on that occasion, and on various occasions since at my request, have gone to him and pointed out to him how unwise it was for him to do anything of the kind. That, however, did not prevent him from going on with this kind of thing, until last summer, an offence of what I regarded as an intolerable character was committed by him. No doubt Mr. Schaffner has heard the words uttered by my hon. friend from Halifax imputing crimes and misdemeanors against this Government, charging the Government with dishonesty and with misappropriating funds; but unlike the hon. members of this House, Mr. Schaffner evidently took those words seriously and believed them; and so I found that last summer, when Americans were coming over to get goods out of the customs house, they were gravely informed by this man that the money he was collecting by way of duty was going to Ottawa to be stolen and that there was a corrupt Government in power. I could not countenance anything of that kind, and I did not think it was just that an officer of that character should be retained in office. Mr. Schaffner was not only guilty of acts of offensive partisanship, but he was guilty of gross irregularities in the conduct of his own office.
Matters were brought to me which, if I had reported them to the department, would have led to an investigation; but, out of consideration for Mr. Schaffner, I put the offence on a milder basis and made the recommendaion I did. I am Teady to stand before my constituents and justify to the limit the action I have taken.
What the hon. minister has stated in reference to the appointment of a successor to this man is absolutely correct. The person appointed temporarily to fill the office is a young man of excellent habits and ability. At the very opening of the war he Offered himself for service abroad, and it was with great disappointment that he found himself turned down. His rejection

was followed 'by a long illness, from which he has just recovered/ He is not now in a condition of health to engage in anything like strenuous work. In the absence of any returned soldier in the constituency, I thought he should have this position temporarily. I went over the list of those from the county of Annapolis who had returned from the front, but found none who would be eligible for this position. Had I found one eligible it is quite likely I should have regarded his claims upon the office as higher than those of the gentleman who received it.
The complaint is made that this officer, Mr. Schaffner, has been dismissed, notwithstanding the fact that lie has a son serving .at the front, a son who has been wounded. I believe that Mt. Schaffner has a son at the front who is doing good service for his country, and that he has received some slight wounds, because of which he has been in the hospital for a short time. But I understand it is nothing very serious, and that he will return to the front shortly.
I congratulate hon. gentlemen opposite on their new-found concern for the soldiers at the front and even for the relatives of those soldiers. Last session my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and other hon. -gentlemen from Nova Scotia seriously attacked, not a relative of a soldier at the front, but actually a gallant soldier himself, who was doing sterling service for his country at that time, and who has since made the supreme sacrifice, has given his life for his country. I refer to the late Mr. Gore Foster, of Halifax. At that time it was incumbent upon me to maintain the cause of a gallant soldier against the very violent attacks of these hon. gentlemen. I am glad their attitude towards the soldier has changed and that, while last session they were ready to attack an absent soldier who was fighting for his country and his flag, and to attack him cn very paltry grounds, they now hold that even the relatives of soldiers are -sacred and shall not be touched, no matter what they do. If the party to which the hon. member for Halifax belongs is sincere, it has an excellent opportunity to show it. At this time there is vacant in the county of Annapolis a position very mhch better than that which Mr. Schaffner has lost, the position of Registrar of Deeds for the county.
If the hon. gentleman is so concerned for Mr. Schaffner, he could show That concern by having him appointed to /this vacant position. A position in the gift
of the Liberal provincial Government. We will wait to see how sincere these hon. gentlemen are in this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton) :

I confess to a feeling of surprise when I heard the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) present facts to show that, even in this time of war, civil servants are dismissed for offences which evidently are hoary with age. I say I was surprised that this should be done at this time, when I myself and every other member of this House holds his seat not by the voice of the people but by the voices of himself and his fellow-members. I concur in everything that was said by the hon. member for Halifax on that subject and hold with him that in view of our present tenure of office we should be very careful as to the scope we give ourselves, and should devote our efforts simply to the accomplishment of those purposes for which this extension of time was given us. But in his zeal for dismissals the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) is only following the example of his party in the province of Nova Scotia. I think the most conspicuous case of dismissal in the province of Nova Scotia was the practical dismissal of our lieutenant governor. When war broke out, we had as lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia a distinguished gentleman who was well qualified for his position and who had taken a particularly active part in providing for the soldiers at the front and those going tc the front. Now, if any officers should be continued in their positions during the period of the war, those officers are the lieutenant governors, and- this is particularly true of the lieutenant governor of Nova Scotia. But we had those who desired his dismissal sitting, as it were, on the steps of Government House at Halifax, watching not merely the calendar but the clock, yes the chronometer, to determine exactly when the lieutenant governor's term expired, according to London time. They would not even wait until business hours of that day in Nova Scotia, but they dismissed him by meridian time at Greenwich. This shows the extreme desire for dismissals in Nova Scotia even in the case of a lieutenant governor -the special representative in the province of His Majesty the King. For their action in this case, I assume, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) himself, is particularly responsible. And with this as expressive of the gospel of the Tory party in Nova Scotia, we need hardly won-

der at what they may do in the case of a mere custom house officer.
But is it not surprising to see the hon. member for Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) descend to such minor things as these? Very few hon. gentlemen in this House * hold the high distinction that he holds as a Canadian statesman. Most of us are ordinary politicians, obliged to give attention to political matters and to look after such things as electoral lists, so that we shall not make any bad friends among the people. But another and higher plane upon which the politician finds no place or standing is that occupied by statesmen. In support of the claim which I make for the hon. member for Annapolis, we have sworn testimony on the records of the High Court in the province of Nova Scotia. That being the case, we expect of him conduct becoming a statesman. Of course, if this evidence went to a jury they might measure it more closely and weigh it more carefully when they were told that this sworn -testimony was the evidence of the hon.. gentleman himself. But it could not be said that the hon. gentleman, when he solemnly swore that he himself was a statesman, was an independent witness. 1 wejl remember meeting the hon. gentleman in my county at a court session, which was largely brought about by the manoeuvering and manipulations of the hon. gentleman when he was attending a local election. While going through my county on that occasion he had a happy faculty of talking glibly about dismissals. His methods were very shrewd. He would go to a postmaster, say, on the north shore in Victoria county and say: You have a post office; you had better vote for our man, and you will hold your office.

maintopic: DISMISSAL OF COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS AT MIDDLETON, N.S.
speechtext: If I heard the hon. member for Annapolis properly, he complained that I said that in the county of .Victoria he was asking people to remain home from voting, on the promise of their getting offices, or on the threat that they would lose their position. I said nothing of' the kind. Unless a guilty conscience accused him, I do not see how that came to the hon. gentleman's mind. I think it is open to members of the House, even jocularly, if you like, to say something about our friends in the House who are zealous in the discharge of their duties, particularly in the matter of dismissals. I was simply observing that my hon. friend had put himself on the pedestal of a statesman, and that the dismissal of a poor old man in the county of Annapolis, after his having been left in office nearly six years after the change of government in 1911, was not the act of a statesman. I was pointing out that my learned friend was not living up to his old oath, when he swore that he was a statesman in the court of Mr. Justice Russell in the province of Nova Scotia. He was asked: Are you a politician?-asked by Mr. Lovett, a gentle-man well known to you Mr. Speaker-are you a politician Mr. Davidson? And he answered: no sir, I -am a statesman. I am looking for great things from great sources; and you will pardon me also when I point out that this proud bird, the eagle, which is [DOT] supposed to deal with this thing, that this great bird, the statesman-eagle of Annapolis, has fallen on such poor, small prey as this ppor man who was dismissed from office. After all we shall come to this conclusion that an insect is still but an insect at most, though it crawl onOhe head of a queen, and after this, notwithstanding the records of Mr. Justice Russel's court and the sworn testimony, we shall have to deal with the member of Annapolis, knowing that he has the same old feet of clay we were accustomed to in the days gone by. We were told that this man Sehaffner had on the morning of the election a woe-begone look on his face. That is the statement made by the hon. member for Annapolis. He had a visage that was simply frightful. Well, I should like to have a snapshot of the two visages on that morning, because up to that time and for several days afterwards the position of the hon. member was very insecure indeed; he held on by a single thread; there were only thirteen very doubtful votes between him and the cold shades of outside, and it was only by a compromise, not by the will of the people of Annapolis, that the hon. member has a . seat in this House.

He travelled on the hearsay evidence of men who came over from the United States, who went to the customs house, and my hon, friend heard them saying that this officer was telling them there were some crooked dealings by this Government, -and that money paid for duties might go in that direction. Schaffner is not in the happy position of my hon. friend who -can come here and, in the high court of Parliament, state his case and justify this dismissal. I accept the statement of the hon. member for Annapolis upon that point. But I do say that if the hon. member did not see fit to justify his recommendation for dismissal upon the ground of official irregularity, he should not resort to that defence here to-day. If that official was guilty of official irregularity, it was only fitting and proper that he should be dismissed. But if my hon. friend had knowledge of these facts, he should have communicated them to the Minister of Customs; an investigation should have been held, and upon such grounds the man should have been dismissed. Personally I am not interested in the welfare. of Mr. Schaffner. He .is absolutely unknown to me.
I made a few observations upon this motion for the purpose of calling to the attention of the House one or two principles that were involved. I say this, that the Government had no right to dismiss an official now or since last October upon the ground of political partisanship unless it was grossly offensive, because the official is in the same position as a member of Parliament, and there has been an under-

standing that when even a vacancy occurs in Parliament to-day the political party holding that seat shall have it filled by another gentleman supporting that party, if the seat is filled at all. I should like to point ont to the hon. gentleman again that the Government is m power to-day,. I assume, with limited powers.
I take it that the extension granted last year was upon the assumption that there should not be an exercise of many of the powers usually exercised during peace time and within the ordinary parliamentary term. I do not find any fault with the statement of the Minister of Customs with respect to what should be the conduct of officials. I think all civil servants should abstain from active political interference. I have always advised any of my own political friends whom I have recommended to office to abstain from political activity, first, because I do not believe in it, and, in the next place, because I have never found their influence of any great value to me. Nor, have I ever observed them to be influential when active for the body who appointed them.
The other principle I wished to impress upon hon. gentlemen was in reference to the fulfilment of their pledges as contained in the orders in council of November, 1915, as amended by the subsequent order in council of October, 1916. The Minister of Customs states that it was not called to his attention that the gentleman appointed had been rejected upon offering to enlist and I am bound to assume that the hon. member for Annapolis never called the attention of the Minister of Customs to this fact.

The circumstances will be explained perhaps mqre clearly in the correspondence which I will read than if I attempted to state them. First, I will read from a letter written by the Rev. Dr. Coffin, formerly of Prince Edward Island, but who is now located at San Famando, Trinidad. He writes on October 14 to a friend of his, a clergyman, in the province of Nova Scotia, as follows:
San Fernando, Trinidad, October 13, 1916.
Dear Mr. Thomson:
I am enclosing you a statement from Jacob Corsbie in regard to his son. His statement will explain the case. His return has caused a great amount of talk and bad feeling. Personally, X do not believe that he was treated fairly, but according to a rule of thumb method of interpreting the Immigration Act. Canadians can hardly be respected abroad if this is a sample of our laws and their working.

[DOT] source that is unquestioned, and I think the Government, now they are brought to their attention, should at once provide for the admission of this young gentleman.
I want to say a word or two generally with reference to the 'law excluding Chinese. In the United States, at their great universities, one finds quite a number of Chinese who have gone there from China to complete their education, and that ought to be our policy in this country. If the Act, and the regulations made under the Act, are not sufficiently wide to admit these people from China who wish to come heie to complete their educational training they should he amended so that there would be no question about the admission of Chinese coming here for that purpose.
I have brought the case of this young man to the attention of the House at the request of some very well-known clergymen in the province of Nova Scotia, who have been connected with the Island of Trinidad The facts are as I have stated, and unless the department has other information justifying their course in this case I submit that some action should be taken by the Government, in order to remove the bad impression which unquestionably exists and will continue to exist in Trinidad in regard to the treatment of this young man.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. ROCHE (Minister of the Interior) :
speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: This case has been dealt with departmentally. Although I am not conversant with all the facts, I had a short memorandum placed in my hands this morning regarding the motion of my hon. friend. I think some of the statements in the correspondence which he has read are grossly exaggerated. When all the facts are brought down I do not think they will substantiate the statements that were read, that this young man has been treated like a criminal. I cannot quite take the hon. gentleman's view that, because certain respectable gentlemen had vouched for this young man and asked for his admission, the Government should therefore have acceded to their request. We frequently get very strong letters asking us to admit certain people who would be barred by the Immigration Act. In regard to this particular case, the reason why this young man was excluded by the officials of the department was that, according to their interpretation of the Act, he did not come within the exemptions. He was of Chinese origin and therefore was excluded under the Chinese Immigration Act. I will read the short memorandum

dealing with this question supplied to me by the Superintendent of Immigration:
Clement Russell Corsbie arrived at St. John, N.B., In September, 1916. While of British nationality, he is of Chinese descent and, not belonging to the exempt classes, could have been legally admitted only upon payment of the $500 head tax. Representations were made to the department by a large number of persons, but as there is no provision in the Chinese Immigration Act for any departure from the terms of same, the department tooli the stand that admission could be only upon payment of the $500 head tax, and as Corsbie was unable to pay, he was deported. Objection to the department's action was made by his father and a rather severe criticism was made in the Presbyterian Witness, published at Halifax. It was pointed out to this paper tnat in their views they should criticize the law, not the administration of the law.
(Sgd.) W. D. Scott, Superintendent of Immigration.
That is the only report that has been placed in my hands. I may say that there, has been some correspondence with the Governor of Trinidad and a courteous letter was sent to him pointing out that owing to the Chinese Immigration Act this young man was refused admission. I quite agree with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) that the admission of young Chinese students into the United States under their immigration law for the purpose of attending any of their universities is more liberal than our law in Canada has been up to the present time. For the last two years I have been discussing the question w)it'h those who have brought the matter to my attention, and I have already prepared an amendment to the Chinese Immigration Act to be submitted this session, to place the admission of these young Chinese students who desire to attend our schools and colleges, on the same footing as in the United States. This was a case where the young man, according to the interpretation of the officials of the department, did not come under any of the exempt classes, and as he did not have the $500 head tax, he was not admitted. Had he paid the $500 head tax, he would have been admitted and he could have attended any of our universities for one year, and on leaving the country afterwards he would have had that head tax refunded. We do that right along. Any young man of Chinese origin who comes to Canada and attends our universities pays the head tax upon admission, and when he leaves the country, the head tax is refunded. That is the difference between the United States law and ours. The United States do not impose the head tax.

Is the wording in the
Chinese Immigration Act:	"Of Chinese
origin "?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I have not the Act here.

Would not that mean
a man born in China, originating in China? The son of a man who has been a British subject for fifty years is surely not of Chinese origin.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The Superintendent of Immigration uses the expression " of Chinese descent The interpretation which the department has placed on the matter-and I think the matter has engaged the particular attention of the department-is that he did not come within any of the exempt classes. That may be wrong and I will have the matter looked into more critically, but I feel sure that no similar case will arise in the future. The Act has not been changed since this Government came into power; this is the manner in which the Act has been administered since it was placed upon the Statute-book, and the same officials are still administering the Act. I quite agree, however, that the Act should be amended and, as I stated before, I have prepared an amendment to be submitted this session.

I think the word in the Act is "origin," and that must mean a man who has been born in China, who is a Chinaman. If tl)e minister is sound in his views, then a man whose great-grandfather happened to be a Chinaman and whose blood might be only about one-tenth Chinese, would be excluded. The Statute surely cannot mean that. In this case the boy was the son of a British subject, a man who had left China when a boy, who had lived in a British colony and w ho had become a British subject. This boy is a British subject; his mother is not a Chinese woman, and his mother's blood must count in considering the question. If the word is "origin," as the minister seems to think it is, it is clear that this boy ought to have been admitted.

The statements that I made in regard to this matter were not comments by myself with reference to anything that occurred at St. John, but were contained in letters which came from Trinidad, and the mention of the manner in which the young man was treated was contained in a letter from the boy's father.
On account of the situation of the library it is difficult to get books outside of those in general use, but my recollection of the

Statute is that a person excluded is a person of Chinese origin, and it seems to me a very fine distinction, when you are dealing with a British subject coming from Trinidad, whose status has been certified to by the Government of that colony, to put him within the terms of the Statute. I would like to know what interpretation would be put upon the right to enter Canada of a person for instance, who had been born of a British father but whose mother happened to be born in China, and who therefore had some Chinese blood in him. Could he be exc'uded under that Statute? He could not be, and if you reverse that condition I think that the same reasoning would apply.
I am glad to hear that the minister recognizes that the law requires to be amended. I would suggest, in order to avoid the feeling of resentment which this matter has caused in Trinidad, on account of the notoriety that has been given to this case, that steps be taken to satisfy the authorities there, in so far as it is possible to do so, as to the regret this country has over the exclusion that has been made.
