Mr. F. F. PARDEE (Lambton West) asked for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public, importance, namely: the proper treatment, care and provision for employment of returned soldiers, and the desirability of appointing a committee of the House to sit during the adjournment, for the purpose of considering this subject and reporting to the House at as early a date as possible.
And leave having been granted,

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt of the fact that while the war and the winning of the war is uppermost in our minds, we have the supreme duty of providing that the men who left comfortable homes, who gave up profitable employment and lucrative positions, who went overseas from a sense of loyalty and devotion, and who were willing when so going to make, if necessary, the great sacrifice, and many of whom have returned to Canada broken in body and health, shall be fitly and properly taken care of by the state. Let me for one moment refer to what these men have done. I quote now from a report submitted by the Canadian War Records Office to the right hon. Prime Minister:-
The duty ot the Records Office was to follow the fortunes of the First Division in
France, to share its experience, and to give to the people of Canada an account of the performances of its regiments; and finally to enshrine in a contemporary history those exploits which will make the First Division immortal. That division stood at Ypres in May, 1915, as the last bulwark of civilization against the triumphant inroads of barbarism. They held the pass and barred the road to Calais.
If the man who made that report had written volumes of the record of the Canadian troops he could not have said more than he has said in those few sentences. When we say that, just let us consider for one moment what the result would have been to Canada and to the Empire had the road to Calais not been blocked. Those men did it, or helped to do it, and to those men our gratitude ought to be due, not in a sentimental way, but in a manner to redound to the credit of the state. These men, when they enlisted and went overseas, did not go to fight for the love of fighting. They went from a sense of loyalty and a sense of duty. They went to preserve 'liberty, to maintain justice, to preserve the very Empire itself, and thus-I am speaking here as a Canadian to Canadians-they have secured for Canada and her people prosperity, contentment and wealth. So far as Canada is concerned, with the exception of those mothers and those fathers who have given their sons to this holy cause, none of us has felt the stress of warfare, all have lived in happiness and contentment. It has undoubtedly been noticed by every member of this House that calls are constantly being sent out for charity for these men. Concerts are given, entertainments are advertised as being for the help of the returned soldiers. Let me just read a statement which I cut from one of the Ottawa papers in answer to a circular that apparently had been distributed throughout this city, asking for help of a charitable kind, such as I have described. Here is a letter from a man with sons at the front.
He says:
I think the conditions revealed in a circular which is being distributed from door to door soliciting aid for our returned soldiers is a disgrace to our country. That the Government should make no provision to aid the returned soldiers who have been rendered unfit for further duty at the front until such time as he would be in a position to help himself, would seem incredible if the information had not come from such a source. If the Government decided that the matter could best be attended to by local boards in the localities whence the soldiers came-why is no provision made to finance such boards?
If the cost is to be a separate charge on the citizens, why not raise the money by

means of taxation, with a poll tax on those who do not otherwise pay taxes?
Many of us are paying from 2 to 2J per cent of our income to the Patriotic Fund. Those of us who have sons at the front would hesitate to assume additional responsibilities to provide for-I shall say-an additional Patriotic Fund. Our own sons may return disabled, and in need of all the assistance we can render in this line.
If the Government of Canada and of the provinces have done as little as one would infer from a perusal of this circular in question-simply authorizing Aid Commissions to solicit charity, or raise money in any old way, I, for one, cannot agree with that part of the circular which says they "have not been unmindful of their responsibilities."
My argument, and I shall state it very shortly, is that no charity should be asked for, or given, to men who have rendered such splendid service to their country. It is degrading to the men, and it is degrading to the people of Canada. I say that those who, during the stress and struggle of the past two and a half years have lived here in peace and happiness and contentment, should not be solicited to contribute towards a fund to provide for returned soldiers, but that they should be made to pay, and to pay proportionately to their worth. That is, I take it, Sir, the real thought of the people of Canada. I believe that this is a matter which is wholly under the control of the Government, and that the Government should take it up at once. A central organization should be established, and that central organization should see to it that every soldier who returns, and every soldier who ought to be helped, is helped in a way that is fit and proper, to the needs of that particular man. I understand that about 200,000 men have left our shores.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: About 300,000, I think.

That makes my argument all the stronger. About 300,000 men have left our shores, and, according to the figures which I have, about 10,600 have returned. There are to-day in England about 12,000 invalided Canadian soldiers, and they will return to Canada at the rate of about 2,000 per month. When the war is over the men will come back at the rate of ten times the number that are coming back to-day, and I say that to subject these returned men to the vicissitudes of such an organization as now exists, will do justice neither to the men themselves nor to the citizenship of this country. We established in the province of Ontario a soldiers' commission under the Act of 1916. That soldiers' com-

mission may be all very well in its way, but in speaking to its chairman in Ottawa, he informed me that on making enquiry the answer he received was: We want you to go on and do as much as you can for these men, and when you have got to the end of your tether we will take the matter up. That is not right. That is absolutely throwing back upon charity the maintenance of these men. In so far as the Ottawa commission is concerned, they tell me that they have absolutely got to the end of their rope. They have found employment, not always permanent, for the men who have returned; but to-day they are up against the fact that they cannot take care of any more returned soldiers. Then you have the Soldiers' Association itself here in Ottawa, and I understand that these soldiers' associations have been established in various centres of Canada. In Winnipeg they have a Soldiers' Association with 1,100 members; in Victoria one with 300 members; in Woodstock one with 150 members; in Vancouver, one with 250 members; in Hamilton, one with 300 members; in Edmonton, one with 300 members; in Calgary, one with 200 members; in Ottawa one with 200 members; in Montreal one with 500 members, and in Toronto, f'ne with 700 members. These men are also endeavouring out of the goodness of their hearts-though so far as I know without financial assistance from the Government-to do what they can to help their comrades who have returned from overseas, but it is plainly evident to any one who will take the trouble to think the matter over for a few minutes that every one of these associations or commissions which I have mentioned must very rapidly come to an end of its resources; and then, forsooth, the soldiers will come back here in a broken and maimed condition, and there will be no proper organization to take care of them. I read from a newspaper published last Saturday:
From London, Ontario, it is reported that Private G. Walton of Windsor, a returned invalided soldier, was without overcoat or gloves, and had his hands frozen at Quebec. He is being cared for in the London hospital, and his case should receive such attention as will make similar cases impossible.
That is one concrete case, and, I have no doubt, there are hundreds of similar cases.
It is not altogether the fault of the commissions because, so far as I can learn, some of the soldiers themselves are not too anxious to be helped, land some of them do as they ought not to do on their return to this c.ountry. Nevertheless, the large proportion of them come back in such a state [DOT]

[DOT]that if properly taken care of they can be made useful to the state and useful to themselves.
A pension scheme has, of course, been established, but I will not weary the House by referring to it in detail because every member is familiar with its provisions. It makes a certain allowance for certain disabilities according to a percentage. In *Class 6, for instance, it provides " Disability under 20 per cent, a gratuity not exceeding $100." That is, if a man comes back 20 per cent less able bodied than when he went away, he is handed $100, and allowed to shift for himself. The men who went overseas were actual economic forces in this country for the good of the country, and if they ihave returned disabled to even a greater extent than 20 per cent, to the extent of 40 per cent or even up to 60 per cent, my contention is that they ought not to be 'allowed to depend merely upon a pension. The man who does nothing, who takes all and gives nothing, is of no use to the country. The Pensions Board ought to see that the men who are injured to the extent of 20, 40, 60, or even 80 per cent are taken in hand, taught some trade, and, as I said before, made of actual good to the country and to themselves; otherwise, it simply means that we will be paying millions of dollars in pensions and receiving absolutely no return therefor. Let me read an instance of what they are doing at St. Maurice in France:
St. Maurice is a hive of workshops of all kinds, shoemaking: shops, machine shops, auto repair shops, blacksmith shops with blazing: forges, and clothes-making shops, and the workmen are the wounded soldiers from the firing line, minus an arm, leg or eye, on which they hacf before depended, but now launched on a new line which did not need that arm, leg or eye.
There is also the other scheme of teaching returned soldiers farming, and with that is coupled the question of land grants. With land grants out and out, I am not in sympathy, as I have before said in this House. Then there is the question of central camps, where the men could be taken to learn a trade, and then afterwards be distributed. These are all things, I submit, Mr. Speaker, which the people of this Dominion want to see attended to, and which it is the bounden duty of the Government to do. I admit that it is a large question. Other countries have had wars, and have had to tackle this same sort of problem, but we must remember that today in Canada we have to get into the way of doing big things. We belong to a mighty empire, and we have to
grow bigger in the bigness of the whole, and if we want to succeed and be the nation that we ought to be, no duty and no obligation should be too great for us to shoulder on behalf of our citizen soldiers. These men are coming back from the front in daily increasing numbers, and so far as I know their care has so far been neglected by the Government. There is no further time to lose. This House will shortly adjourn for, I suppose, two or three months. In that time valuable information might be collected and valuable statistics gathered by a committee that should be appointed for that purpose. The committee could make a report which would be available for the benefit of the House when it re-assembles. It appears to me that now is the time to take action. No further time should be wasted, for every day that is lost means just that much the worse for the men who return from fighting our battles.
My own opinion is, if I may venture to give it to the House, that a Federal Commission composed of men of the highest standing with broad and full authority should be appointed by the Crown to continue for a period of say five years after the conclusion of peace, for the purpose of dealing with these questions. The commission should, of course, have an efficient staff and equipment. At each provincial capital and at one or more important points in the provinces from which enlistments have been greatest, sub-commissioners or agents should be appointed. They should be required to make frequent reports to the chief commissioners, not only on subjects of which the commission might seek information, but also upon all matters coming to their notice or in any way relative to returned soldiers. This would prevent overlapping of work between Dominion and provincial commissioners in case the provinces undertook in their own way to deal with the situation. Wherever also city or other municipal commissions have been or will be established the federal office should be in close touch with these also.
In conclusion, I again urge that this should be made a Government matter for which the Government should be responsible; that the funds required whatever they may be, should not in any way be allowed to be solicited or distributed in a way which savours of charity, and that whatever moneys are necessary for carrying on the work successfully should be made part of

the national debt of Canada for which the people of this country would be responsible.
There can be no question, there is none in my own mind at least, that were this done it would be an aid to recruiting. There are instances within my own personal knowledge, and undoubtedly there are hundreds of others, where recruiting to the extent of at least two or three men has been hindered by the fact that no sufficient provision is made for returned soldiers. When the war ends the need will be greater than it is to-day, or than it has been, and I say that we should guard ourselves against that day, so that when it does come we should be at least in a partial condition and in a partial state of readiness to take care of the men when they come.
I cannot close my remarks better, Sir, than by reading the following paragraph in the Ottawa Soldiers' Aid Commission literature.
Our duty to them is clear. They have been our substitute on the battlefields of Prance and Flanders. They have suffered in our behalf. Their bodies have been maimed in our defence. On us rests the high and sacred obligation of making their future lives reasonably comfortable and as useful as possible.
I wanted to know about what was the actual amount.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It varies in different cases. I really have not that detail, but when this matter goes before a com-

mittee, as it certainly shall in view of the suggestion of the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee), all these matters will be submitted in the greatest possible detail by the officers of the Military Hospitals Commission.
Another and an important question, which has been raised by the hon. member who has made the motion, is the introduction of the men who are returning to employment. Employment is in one sense a provincial or local matter, although I do not for one moment desire to minimize the responsibility of the Federal Government for assisting in the matter. There was a conference between the Federal Government and the provincial governments in October, 1915, and the view then taken, without dissent, as I understand, was that, for the time being at least, the question of finding employment should be undertaken and dealt with by the provincial governments. I shall quote textually the memorandum which was agreed upon between the Governments as represented by the head of the Military Hospitals Commission and the representatives of the various provincial governments. That memorandum is textu-aliy as follows:
The Government of each province should appoint a central provincial committee consisting of such number of members as each province may deem advisable.
All expenditures necessary in connection with the organization and administration of provincial and. other purely local committees should be borne by the provincial or local [DOT] authorities, or by voluntary contributions.
Each of the provinces of Canada, working through its central committee, should assume the responsibility of endeavouring- to find employment for discharged soldiers, who, upon their return to Canada, are physically and otherwise fit to assume such employment. All expenditures necessary in undertaking the duty should he borne by the province.
That was the memorandum agreed upon; that was the scheme prepared at that time and the scheme which has since been carried out. Therefore, the situation resolved itself upon t-hiat basis in this way: As to men returning to Canada who are of the convalescent class, they were taken charge of by the Military Hospitals Commission, and in so far as might be advisable or possible, they received training or education which would be of use to them upon their ultimate discharge. So far as concerns the men who were disabled and thereby incapable of resuming their former occupations, the Military Hospitals Commission undertook to make provision for the necessary training, and also to provide for their families in the

period in which such training was being received. Then as to those who do not come back ,as convalescents-
Is any part of that expense borne by the provincial governments?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
The educational expenses are entirely borne by the Dominion?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All borne by the Federal Government, as I understand it.
Thus, we have the convalescents who are receiving treatment in hospitals; we have those who are discharged from hospitals but are not disabled and who receive training under the direction of the Military Hospitals Commission, and thirdly, we have those who desire to engage in some employment, and as to those one might look at the situation in a double aspect.
Some of those men who have returned from the front came back to positions which were held open for them after their enlistment, and they are not included in the figures which I am about to give. In fact, I have not before me any statistics with regard to the number of men of that class. But I am about to give some statistics which have been furnished by the secretaries of the Provincial Employment Commissions, and I venture to think that the amount of work which they have accomplished in this connection will be a surprise to most of the members of this House, and perhaps to the people of this country. I have from all nine provinces returns which have been furnished to me by the secretary of the Military Hospitals Commission. They are divided into three classes:-the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found; the number of returned soldiers who are still unemployed; and the number of men discharged from the camps without going overseas, for whom employment has been found.
In the province of Prince Edward Island, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is six; the number for wnom employment has not been found is five. In Nova Scotia the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 307. and the soldier for whom employment has not been been found is 15. In New Brunswick, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 190, and the number for whom employment has net been found is 60. In Quebec, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment

has been found is 1,438, and the number for whom employment has not been found is six. In Ontario, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 1,750, and they have no record of any soldier for whom employment has not been found. That is, there is no returned soldier unemployed. In Manitoba, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 633, and they make no report of any who is not employed. In Saskatchewan, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 424, and there is no return of any for whom employment has not been found. In Alberta, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 621, and there are 23 for whom employment has not been found. In British Columbia, the number of returned soldiers for whom employment has been found is 517, and the number for whom employment has not been found is 39. Taking these totals, we find that employment has been found for 5,886 returned soldiers, and that there are 148 in the various provinces for whom employment has not yet been found.
Do these figures apply to discharged soldiers?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: YTes.
Do I understand my right hon. friend to say that there are only 148 returned soldiers in all the provinces for whom employment has not been found?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the statement made to me on the reports to the secretary of the Military -Hospitals Commission by the various provincial committees.
Is that up to the end of 1915?	.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is up to the 3rd of February of this year. This information is based upon reports made to the secretary of the Military Hospitals Commission by the various provincial committees which were constituted under the arrangement made in October, 1915, at the conference between the Federal authorities and the provincial authorities. I should add that the secretary of the New Brunswick Provincial Commission states that work can be found for all returned soldiers. That province has 60 unemployed men, but it is not anticipated that they will be out of employment for very long. The secretary of the Soldiers' Aid Commission of Ontario reports that no discharged soldiers able to
work are out of employment, and that there are 150 vacancies now on file. That is, there are opportunities for employing 150 men if they are available. The secretary of the Saskatchewan Provincial Committee states that there are practically no returned soldiers out of employment, although the problem of procuring light employment is becoming very difficult.
In addition, in New Brunswick, employment has been found for fifty camp men; that is, men discharged from one or other of the military camps without going overseas. In Ontario, 550 such men have found employment, in Saskatchewan, 34, and in British Columbia 44 such men have procured employment through the provincial committees. If we add these figures, as received from the various provincial committees, we find that there is a total of 678 camp men, for whom employment has been found, and if that number be -added to the 5,886 returned soldiers for whom employment -has been found through the various provincial committees, we have a total of 6,564 men who enlisted, who have been discharged and for whom employment has been found, while, so far as returns from the various provinces show, there are only 148 men for whom, up to the present, employment has not been found.
I -should observe that while the Military Hospitals Commission, itself does not undertake any responsibility with regard to employment, that commission does furnish the secretary of every provincial commission with a record of every man returning to the province in question. Shortly before each man is discharged from an hos

pi-tal or convalescent home, a notification is sent to the -secretary of the provincial committee so that, if possible, a situation may be in readiness for him on his return to civil life. It is also stated in the memorandum, from which I am quoting, that the pay and allowances given to the man in advance, on his discharge, are to enable him to look around for satisfactory employment. It also observes that many men go -back to their former situations, but th-at these men are not included in the statement which I have just read giving the total number of men for whom employment has -been found by the provincial -committees. The memorandum which I have before me -speaks with very great appreciation of the splendid manner in which the provincial- ' governments have responded to the present need, and expresses the opinion that as the need becomes more

acute the provinces wi'l be ready to redouble their efforts.
I may also add that the Government have not lost sight of the fact that there are many openings in the Federal service which may be filled by returning soldiers. It was my expectation to have this afternoon a -statement showing the number of returned soldiers who have 'been appointed to positions in the Federal service. I am informed that in one department alone at least 120 have been appointed. I have given directions to have the information furnished, and by the time the committee has undertaken its work, that information will also be available.
Orders in council, making provision for giving preference to returned soldiers in the Federal service have been passed, and, if I am not mistaken, have all been brought down. My hon. friend also alluded to the question of pensions.
Has the question of establishing permanent soldiers' homes been considered?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think that that has yet been taken up, but it may be a proper matter for the consideration of the committee who will look into the whole subject. With regard to pensions, the subject was under consideration by a committee last session of Parliament, and I need hardly say that the members of that committee devoted themselves to the very important duty which they were called upon to discharge, with greait earnestness, great energy, and great zeal. The report which they made was embodied in an order in council. That order in council was passed, of course, merely as a temporary measure, and it was quite understood that a Bill would be introduced this session. This Bill is in course of preparation, and will be brought down, I hope, at an early date, and I have it in mind that after the Bill is brought down it should be referred to the same committee which had the matter under consideration laeit year. They devoted a great deal of time to the subject land became thoroughly acquainted with it, and any suggestions for modifications of the report they then made should be considered by that committee in the first instance.
I understand that a Pensions Board has been appointed since last session.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, upon the recommendation of the committee. The

members are Mr. J. K. L. Ross, Colonel Labatt and Major Todd.
Would the right hon. gentleman consider whether the French-Cana-dian element might not be represented on that board?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That will be a matter for consideration. The board was not appointed to represent any particular district, any particular class, or any particular race, and, in appointing it we endeavoured to select the best men available. The suggestion of my hon. friend will of course be considered.
Can the Prime Minister give us any information as to the number of pensions distributed to the different ranks.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have not that information with me, but I think it can be easily obtained. In conclusion, I merely wish to add a word with reference to some criticism which has been made over delays occurring in the payment of the first pension cheque. The amount of labour involved in dealing with pensions, particularly in the earlier activities of the pensions board, has, of course, been very great, because the Board had not only to undertake and carry out new duties, but was also confronted with the task of establishing a very considerable organization while its ordinary, every-day work was being carried on. I understand, however, that the system which is being adopted will lead to very much less delay than has sometimes occurred in the past. I do not know if there is any further information I can give to the House at the moment, but it would be proper and appropriate for me to say that I entirely agree in and appreciate the remarks which were made by my hon. friend from West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) in proposing his motion, as to the splendid patriotism of the men who have enlisted in the Canadian overseas forces, and who, by their valour and heroism at the front, have brought such splendid distinction to the country they represent. I quite agree with him also that the country must do all that is reasonable and just to take every care of these men upon their return to Canada, and that, I am assured, will be the spirit in which every member of the House will approach the consideration of this question.

Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted

to make a few observations on this subject I would say that I think the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) is to be congratulated on having brought this matter to the attention of the House, and the House is to be congratulated on the very full information which the Prime Minister has seen fit to give in regard to this question, which is of such great importance to the people of Canada to-day. I know that this information will be gratefully received throughout the country, because there has been considerable curiosity and a good deal of unrest among many of our people as to just what treatment was being accorded our returned soldiers who had seen active service at the front and had been discharged by reason of wounds or -some other disability.
I think the remarks of my hon. friend from West Lambton were intended to relate particularly to those who had been discharged from overseas service as medically unfit, rather than to those who are receiving medical, hospital, or surgical treatment at the present time. There have been a great many eases of men who have -served overseas, and who, though not actually wounded, have been rendered medically unfit and been discharged from further service. The treatment of these men, or some of them at -all events, -has not been as generous as it might have been. I think my hon. friend from West Lambton referred particularly to those men who had been discharged and who took a ten dollar bill or a fifty dollar bill, or the maximum of one hundred dollars, on being discharged from further service through no fault of their own, but merely because from some cause or another they had become medically unfit. Cases have come to my own knowledge of such men, and these cases involve considerable hardship. In one case a man who had a wife and nine children resident in Canada was discharged on the 20th of May last. Upon his dischargee in England he received $100. He was not returned to Canada until September. Upon his return home he found his wife and family at their last resource; they had even sold the household furniture. The man himself, when he landed at Guelph, where he had formerly lived, was absolutely without a dollar, and isaw nothing in sight. He had to be assisted subsequently, and two or three months afterwards he obtained employment as a guard at the provincial institution. I have in mind three cases similar to that I have just mentioned, and I have given this case to illustrate the difficulty to which I
think my hon. friend from West Lambton intended to direct the attention of the House, namely, the treatment of men who are returned to Canada before employment is found for them. Their lot is a hard one. Some of them come back none too well clad, and the majority of them without any money at all. One man who had been discharged in England as medically unfit, on landing at Halifax, received $100. Another, -some months after his return, received from the department $50, and that man has no employment yet, and he lives in Ontario. This period between the discharge of a man and the day when he obtains employment is certainly a hard time for him, and if married for his family as well.
The news which the Prime Minister has given the House in regard to conditions in Ontario is most gratfying to me, and I am sure the whole province will 'be gratified to hear that every returned soldier who is fit for work has had employment offered to him, and that there are in Ontario to-day no less than 150 vacant positions which can be filled by returned soldiers, according to the return which I understand, is brought down to the first day of the present month of February. 1 will certainly take the opportunity of notifying two men whom I have in mind that they had better file their applications with the provincial authorities at once. Every one realizes that the task before the Government and before the country in dealing with the returned soldier is going to be serious, more serious next year than this, most serious when demobilization really sets in. I listened with the greatest interest to the scheme outlined by the Prime Minister this afternoon, and if I had any criticism whatever to offer in regard to it, it would be that it is rather involved: there are too many commissions and sub-commissions, too many divisions and subdivisions. I think it will take some time to work out the scheme, and during the interim there is going to be a great deal of hardship suffered by soldiers on their return to Canada. My suggestion-and I give it only as a suggestion-is that the Government would do well to take some definite step now in regard to vocational training. We are going to have a very large number of men -suffering from total permanent disability, who will never be able to earn their living again and who will no doubt in many cases be absolutely dependent upon their pensions; but for men who are only partially disabled, dismembered or blind of an

eye, steps should be taken immediately by the Government, and I do not believe in deputing that work to the provincial governments or to any other body. I believe a commission should be formed by this Government, and the formation of a commission, if a commission be thought desirable, should not be delayed, but the work should be undertaken in the very near future. My right hon. friend says that some vocational specialists, some technical specialists, would doubtless have to be employed for such a purpose. Let them be employed, They can be procured.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They have been procured.
Let them get to work now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They are at
work.

Let the Government
adopt the necessary means to put into application whatever is determined upon by those vocational specialists. This Parliament surely can grant the money for such a purpose, to establish in the immediate future, say during the coming summer, a very broad comprehensive scheme of vocational training, where the services of men who .have lost an eye or of men who have been partially dismembered, may in the future be usefully employed. The time to start is immediately. It takes time to work the matter out. but if 'started during the present 'spring, by next autumn, when there will be large numbers of men available to take courses at such an institution, that institution can render a tremendous benefit to this country and to the individual who has the benefit of a course in it.
I am not quite as enthusiastic as some people are in regard to the number of returned soldiers who will settle on the land and become agriculturists. Agriculture is a business that must be learned 5 p.m. just as any other business, and while a number of returned soldiers will certainly take advantage of an opportunity to go upon the land, I do not think there will be any great rush of returned soldiers upon the land unless the inducements are very great, and unless men have had some previous training in agriculture or unless their minds naturally turn that way I do not think that the land question is going to offer more than a partial solution of the difficulties which will confront Canada when, demobilization takes place. At the present time, I am satisfied

that the Government has made a splendid showing in regard to its treatment of the injured, of those suffering either from wounds or disease, and I am satisfied that our hospital system, our medical and surgical treatment, and the provision made in this country for tubercular patients on their return from the front are up-to-date and a credit in every respect to the Government. But I do feel that a little more might be done, even as a mere welcome to the man who comes back to this country medically unfit, to keep that man going until his own particular province shall have provided him with an opportunity of obtaining a position. Having regard to the figures submitted to the House to-day, we have nothing to complain of in Ontario. I hope that will continue; I doubt if it will continue because the number of returned 'soldiers will increase in the future; but for that short period from the time when they arrive in Canada until they obtain positions, those men and their families should not suffer for one moment of time.

Mr. Speaker, I think the House and the country are indebted to the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) for the discussion which has been started this afternoon. No one would have walked the hospitals of Europe during the past year and seen the torn and broken men who a few months ago left thi's country in the fullness of health and strength without realizing that a terrible problem confronts Canada and the British Empire in the absorption of the men who have fought on our behalf. The more pne thinks of the problem, the *more difficult the solution becomes ; and if my opinion is worth anything, I think it will take the best judgment and the best brains of this country as well as of other parts of the British Empire, to make adequate provision for those who, the world admits, have done their duty in fighting for the cause of the Empire. But I think the hon. member for West Lambton forgets somewhat or is not aware of what has already been done. I am inclined to think that not many ,of the men who have returned from the front are going to be prepared to go on the faTm. When I was in England and France and Belgium, I spoke to many men as to what their ambitions for the future were, and the general trend of opinion was that the men wanted to return to the place from which they had come and to go back to the work they knew best. It is simple enough to say: Send a man out on the farm; but if a man knows noth-

ing about farming-and farming to-day is a science, just as many other occupations are-he is not going to be able to earn an adequate living, and if a man cannot earn an adequate living on a farm, he is not going to stay out there simply for the joy of living in the country, and I think that statistics will go to show that of all the men who have returned to Canada, not more than three per cent have expressed their willingness to go on the farm. Therefore, I think a problem that confronts us is this: What steps are we going to take to secure employment for the men who have gone from ,our shores? As a member of the Soldiers Aid Commission in the province of Ontario

and I use the word "aid" rather than the word "employment" as used by the Premier-I may say that at its early meetings it realized the problem which it had to face, and upon inquiry it soon came to the conclusion that if we were adequately to meet the situation, it was necessary that we should have the co-operation of local boards throughout the province and that we should have the sympathy and the co-operation of the employers. With that end in view the commission set to work to have subsidiary boards established in the larger centres from which more than five soldiers had left for overseas, and at the present time I think there are some fifty-three bodies in Ontario adequately doing the work for which they were constituted. My information is the same as that given by the Prime Minister-that to-day there are vacancies that cannot be filled because the men are not to be had, and that any soldier who wants work and is willing to work can find a position if he applies to the Soldiers' Aid Commission. The commission does not stop altogether at securing employment for these men. The Commission has authority " to care for and find employment for the members of the Canadian Expeditionary Force," and by the Statutes of 1916 that power was further extended, so that they have power to care for and find employment for the members of His Majesty's Imperial Forces who went overseas. We are going further than finding employment for these men. If a man comes back so broken that it is impossible for him to get work at his former occupation, the Government of Ontario have placed at the disposal of the commission the technical institutions throughout the province, and a great number of these men are being re-educated under the auspices of the Commission. The commission is making provision also for the maintenance and subsistence of a man's
family while he is being re-educated. If it should happen that a man is in a place where work is not available, and work is available at another place, the commission will send the man to the place where work is to be had. The commission makes loans to men to carry them over temporary embarrassments. So, the situation in Ontario is governed most satisfactorily.
I desire to touch for a moment on a misapprehension which exists in the public mind. Let me quote to the House a statement which appeared, I am sure by inadvertence, in the Evening Journal of 21st January last:
The Government so far recognizes no responsibility towards the man who enlisted in the Expeditionary Force and who developed some disease before he left Canada, although this may have arisen from the hardships and exposure attendant upon the performance of his military duties.
That is a misapprehension of the facts. The Military Hospitals Commission takes care of a man who breaks down from exposure, even though he should go no further than the place in which he was enlisted. Such a man is treated with exactly the same consideration as is the man who has been wounded in battle. The original pension scheme made a distinction between the man who had been wounded in battle and the man who was injured in some other way, but the present order in council makes no distinction. Once a man dons His Majesty's uniform he becomes, so to speak, a ward of the state, and if through exposure, exertion, disease or accident, he becomes a less fit man that he was before he enlisted, he thereby becomes entitled to a pension as if he had been wounded on the field.
Complaints have been made in the past of delays in the granting of pensions. In certain cases, such complaint may have been justified. The pension problem is a new problem for Canada, and, in the nature of things, a certain time must elapse before the complex machinery of the new system can be made( to work smoothly. But the organization to-day is so perfected that there is no cause for delay. If a man is entitled to a pension, that pension should be promptly granted to him. There have been cases in which a break occurred between the time when a man's pay and allowances expired and the time when his pension began. But negotiations are now under way to evolve a scheme by which pay and allowances will continue until the pension is granted, so that there will be no time

when the disabled man will not receive either his pay and allowances or his pension.
Among the problems that the Pensions Board or the Hospitals Commission will have to face is that of the men who have suffered impairment not amounting to full disability. I think that in Canada we are going to be met very often with this class of case. A man has lost a limb by explosive bullet, shrapnel or otherwise, and has been treated in a convalescent hospital. After treatment he is discharged as fit for work. But when he is thrown into the hurly-burly of industrial life, nerves that had been frayed by exposure in the trenches are going to break, and the man will be unfitted for his occupation. We shall have to face the problem of the man who has been discharged as not entitled to a pension, but who, as subsequent experience shows, is so broken in his health that he must have hospital treatment. I think the Government of Canada will have to meet the situation and that it will be prepared to meet it by taking that man into the hospital and giving him the treatment necessary to restore him, as far as possible, to health and strength. Another problem we shall have to meet is the question of what may be called functional education as distinguished from vocational education. Hundreds of men will come back to this country not much impaired, if you take the mere capacity to work as a standard, but very considerably impaired in relation to the occupation which they followed before enlisting. I have a case in mind, that of a man who, before he went to the front, followed the trade of a boilermaker. He was hit in the right shoulder and an important muscle and nerve was injured. He is as well as ever, apparently, but when he raises his hand above his shoulder, the power to bring it down with the old-time force is gone. He says: I am only entitled to a small pension, because constitutionally I have made a substantial recovery; but because of the injury that I have suffered, I can only earn a labourer's pay, although, before I went to the front, I earned the pay of a skilled mechanic. By a course of functional education, the injured nerve and muscle might be restored to strength. We must consider the question of functional training.
When one visits the Old Country, he realizes the effort that is being made to place the injured soldiers in useful oecupa-

tions. Our problems are not greater than theirs, but the steps they are taking are an example to us of what can be done. You see there men who have been trained to engage in some lighter occupation than that to which thy were accustomed. You see men who have lost one arm, or perhaps part of a hand, who have been fitted and trained to do as much work as one so injured can possibly do.
In closing, I wish to say, as I said in the beginning, that I believe this country is willing that money should be spent and effort made so to provide that the men who have given to Canada a place among the nations of the world, and who have come back either broken or injured, shall suffer as little as possible for the sacrifices they have made. Because, when the last word is said, they have taken our places in the trenches, and those of us who have remained at home should be only too willing to pay, and pay well.

I am going to take a somewhat critical position, as I think becomes a member of this side of the House; and, while I have nothing but praise for the very full statement given by the Prime Minister, and for the terms of that statement, yet I would venture this criticism: that in dealing with this subject we have been dealing with it as though it were a matter that was not urgent, a matter that was not present; we have been dealing with it as something that might arise, yet might not arise. And the consequence is tha t tremendous hardship has been caused to individuals and tremendous discredit to the Dominion of Canada, simply because we have not done what we ought to have done and what we must do in time. When the war broke out and we sent 33,000 *men to take part in that war, we knew that we would have broken men; we knew that we would have need for provision as to pensions, vocational training, hospital treatment and employment for returned soldiers. But we did not take at that time the steps that we should have taken; we did not take them a year after, or the year after that. We are taking them only now, when the problem has become tremendous, when the discredit has been established, when untold injury has been done to the military and patriotic enthusiasm of the people by the neglect of men who have served our country and to whom our country desires to give every consideration. Because of the policy

of " wait and see a policy which so nearly destroyed the British Empire-we have had [DOT]in Canada these unfortunate cases.
The hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) has drawn attention to the fact that in many cases .a long interval has occurred between the shutting off of the ex-soldier's [DOT]pay and the receiving of his pension. I [DOT]shall not enlarge upon that; I simply say that within my own knowledge there have been such cases, deplorable and discreditable, which have been seriously detrimental to the credit of our country and to the military enthusiasm of our people. I shall not go into details'; they would be harrowing, and would not add to the facts of the case. In my judgment there is no excuse for that condition. The hon. member for Kingston will distinctly remember that that question came up for consideration before the Pensions Committee last year, and that we were at the point of making a recommendation that the pay should continue until the pension began. Upon representation being made to us, however, that that condition would be provided for, we did not put in the recommendation. That is my recollection of the matter.
Another point to which due regard has not been given is this : When a man is discharged without pension, he is discharged because of his unfitness to do the work that we wanted him to do and that he offered to do for us. On the face of it, that is evidence that the man's condition is not . such as will enable him to have an equal standing with his competitors in the labour field. I consider that the authorities have been unduly regardless of the facts in shutting off such a man's pay, giving him $10 and a ticket home, and saying: "We do not know you any longer." A man has a family dependent upon him is discharged from military service because he is not fit, physically, mentally or otherwise, to continue in that employ. That is to say, his power or ability to maintain his family is not as it was when he entered our employ, because at that time we took the responsibility of accepting his services in the belief that his physical and mental ability was at a maximum.
Does the hon. gentleman refer to a man who went overseas and returned?

Yes. Having discharged
this man, we say:	"We do not owe you
anything; we give you no consideration." Even if a man has no dependents at all, he
is apt to be placed in the position of a vagrant-as a matter of fact, cases of this kind have occurred-but if he has a family, as in the case, which has been mentioned, of a man with a large number of children, the condition is very much worse. I think that the authorities would do themselves and the country credit if, when they are giving these men their discharges, they do something to help them through the period of difficulty and straitened circumstances which often follows the cutting off of their soldiere' pay and the discontinuance of the separation and Patriotic Fund allowances to their families. We have been proceeding altogether too much upon the assumption that we are dealing with soldiers as the word "soldier" was understood in former days. We are not dealing with soldiers as that word was understood; we are dealing with citizens, and we should deal with them from the standpoint of their citizenship and of their value to the community as citizens.
It seems to me that the Government should long ago have made provision for those totally disabled soldiers who, being unable to take care of themselves, have no relatives, or whose relatives are not in a position to take care of them. This could be accomplished by establishing a number of soldiers' homes, such as the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) spoke of during the course of the debate on the Address. Most harrowing cases have come to my attention; I shall not trouble the House with the details of them. I think that the Government has not been well advised in making no provisions for taking proper care of these men.
In regard to vocational training, I had the honour to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister last year the fact that at Edmonton we have a technical school that is available for this work. I do not think that it has yet been availed of, and I would respectfully suggest, if it be in order, that this school, as well as others throughout the country, be availed of to this end.

Before you put the motion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister a matter, which, perhaps, is not connected with the subject introduced by the member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee). In a number of the provinces of Canada, if not in all of them, the distinction between real property and personal property has been done away with in dealing with the estates of deceased persons. But the law with regard to holograph and nuncu-

paitive wills has been preserved, and that law provides in my province of Saskatchewan and I think also in Ontario, that the holograph or nuncupative will of a 'Soldier shall deal only with personal property. There is apt to be confusion in the minds of the soldiers and the public in the belief that the holograph and nuncupative wills of soldiers deal with all their property as any other wills would do. I wish to make the suggestion to the Government that it make inquiry as to the facts I have stated, and that the request be made to the legislatures of the various provinces in which this distinction is still preserved that the law be so amended that the holograph and nuncupative will of a deceased soldier shall include realty as well as personal property.

This would
