speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. member for Carleton asked as to the changes in the Ross rifle since the outbreak of war. I am informed that all the changes which have taken place are of a very minor character and are as follows:
Butt trap spring strengthened. Change recommended October 16, 1914, by the Small Arms Committee.
Extractor cut shortened to prevent bolt head turning over. Change reoommended by the Small Arms Committee, April 10, 1915.
Strap of piling swivel strengthened. Change recommended by the Small Arms Committee, April 10, 1915.
Rear end of receiver to be rounded. Change recommended by the Small Arms Committee, June 2, 1915.
New pattern nose cap. Change recommended by the Small Arms Committee, June 11, 1915.
Chamber enlarged to .464 to facilitate extraction. Change authorized in July, 1915, and again in August, 1915.
Removal of sling swivel from trigger guard. Change recommended by Small Arms Committee, November 29, 1915.
The screws were rim punched to prevent them working loose. Change made upon advice from *overseas.
Bolt stop with larger striking surface. Change recommended by the Small Arms Committee, June 11, 1916.
The cavity in the butt for the oil well was deepened 1 inch, making it 8 inches in depth in the wood. Change recommended by the Small Arms Committee, June 30, 1916.
As I have said, I am informed by the Master General of the Ordnance that the changes are all of a very trivial and minor character.

Would the Prime
Minister tell us exactly where the Government and the country stand with reference to the question of the Ross rifle? Are we to understand that notice of a formal nature has been given to the Ross Rifle Company under the contract of the intention of the Government to ask them to manufacture a rifle similar to the Lee-Enfield rifle, but that no order has been given to the company for .any definite number of rifles?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: YTes, that is the situation.

Having regard to the manifest desirability of having the manufacture of arms in this country, and, more particularly, in view of the situation in the country to the south of us, whence the supply of arms will no doubt be cut off on account of their own necessities-does the right hon. gentleman regard that as a desirable situation? Can he not conceive of the possibility of conferring with the Ross
Rifle Company, and obtaining some definite statement as to the number, in order to hasten the manufacture of those rifles upon a larger scale than 10,000, which was intended to be the minimum in peace time? Is there not a way in which. the matter could be hastened so that the country might know that this matter is being taken care of? As it is, both parties seem to be at arm's length. My hon. friend from Carle-ton (Mr. Carvell) suggested that if there was any difficulty the Government could solve it by expropriating the factory. The matter seems to have come to a standstill without the exercise of that authority which the Government manifestly have in war time. The matter seems to have got to a stage where nobody is moving, and no preparation is being made for the future.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think there is any detriment to the public interest in the delay which has taken place. As a matter of fact, I have already pointed out that it is impossible to give an order until we get the drawings and specifications which were asked for in September last, but which have not yet been received. The question is as to what the Government should undertake in the production of rifles, having regard to' the fact that a very large number of rifles already manufactured will probably be on hand at the end of the war, and that these will be suitable for training purposes. After the conclusion of the war we may expect that training purposes. alone will have to be considered for some years. Gn the other hand as I have already pointed out, there is the fact that undoubtedly the Ross Rifle Company has made a very large expenditure for the purpose of producing rifles on a large scale during the war, and while it is manifestly impossible for the Government to continue to give orders on a war scale in time of peace, nevertheless it is proper for the Government to have such consideration for that expenditure ias would .not result in marked injustice or unfairness to the interests which have made that expenditure. That is the .situation which confronts the Government to-day. It is one that is not free from difficulty, and one to which the best possible consideration will be given.

On Friday, in the explanation which he gave upon the subject, my right hon. friend stated to the House that an order in council had been passed fixing the time when the new type of rifle was to be manufactured by the Ross

Rifle Company. The order in council went on to say this:
And that the contractor and the said company he required, on and after the first day of December, 1917, to make all rifles supplied under the said contract to correspond to such last mentioned substituted standard sample rifle the Government undertaking to protect the contractor and his assignee against any actions for infringement of patents as stipulated by the contract, and, moreover, that the Minister of Militia and Defence be authorized to give a notice In the form hereto annexed to the said Sir Charles Ross and his assignee, The Ross Rifle Company.
Are we to understand that no action has been taken by the Company to have rifles manufactured under the terms of this order in council?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say what the company have done. We have given notice that after the date mentioned the rifles to be produced must be of the new type, but we have not yet given an order for the reason I have mentioned: that we have not yet received the drawings and specifications which are necessary for the purpose of giving such an order. The reason why we have not yet. received the drawings and specifications is explained in the tee-gram which I read to the committee on Friday last.	-

About this question of the Ross rifle I wish to say that I altogether object to the Government doing business with a private company for the production of munitions of war such as rifles. I believe that rifles for the purposes of war should be made in a public arsenal on plans devised by our own engineers and experts in the manufacture of rifles, and that we should not be bound, as we are said to be bound, by a contract with the Ross Rifle Company. I want to say further that in view of the statements that were made in this House when the Ross rifle contract was first entered into, some of them by hon. gentlemen associated with the present Government, and in view also of the experience on the battlefields of Europe where the Ross rifle was thrown away by ojir soldiers as being a bad weapon, their lives being in jeopardy, I do not think we ought to pay another dollar to the Ross Rifle Company. To test the feeling of this committee, I propose to move an amend-mend adding Clause 4 to the resolution to this effect:
(4) That none of the money so raised or voted shall be used for the purchase of Ross rifles.

The people of Canada are more than dissatisfied with the experience of Canada in connection with the Ross rifle. The people of Canada are in favour of the starting of a national arsenal for the manufacture of rifles by ourselves, and they are in favour of the elimination of the whole question of profit in connection with munitions. On my own behalf, on behalf of my constituency which has had rather a wide experience with the Ross rifle, and on behalf of our soldiers who have been to the front and who discarded the Ross rifle, I think this contract ought to come to an end here and now, and that not another dollar ought to be paid to this company for those rifles. I therefore move the amendment which 1 have just read.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
I am not sure that the amendment is in ordeT. but assuming for the moment that it is, it seems to me impossible for the committee to adopt it, iand for this reason.: The provision which is included with respect to the Ross rifle is not in respect of any further order, but is in respect of an order already given, and upon which the company is already engaged. It is estimated that about 80,000 rifles under the order given in February, 1916, will remain to be delivered after the end of the present fiscal year. The Government having given that order, and thus having entered into a contract for those rifles, is under obligation to pay for them; the rifles must be paid for unless the good faith of the country is to be called in question, or unless in the meantime some other type of rifle may be substituted for them, and I do not think that that is possible within the period mentioned.

I do not wish to be a
party to voting for the breaking of any contract that this Government has entered into in good faith, but I am bound to say that in my judgment the contract entered into was an unjustifiable and improvident contract, judged from every point of view, and I could not conscientiously vote for the payment of any money on that contract. The suggestion that has been made that the contract should be changed is the proper one, I submit, so that the rifles supplied should be Lee-Enfields instead of Ross rifles. Under these circumstances we should be getting value for our money, and the country would get rifles that could be used. The suggestion that it takes a year or any such long period of time to make the change for which provision was

*made in the original contract entered into *so many years ago is, I think, not borne out by the experience we have had in the making of munitions of all kinds throughout the Empire and the United States. There is no manner of doubt in my mind that if the diligence had been used we could have been making Lee-En-fields now at the Ross rifle factory, and if the Government should he put up against ft by a vote of this House I believe they could yet get Lee-Enfie'lds made at the Ross rifle factory in time to meet the needs of the war. Therefore, for my part, I am going to support the amendment of the hon. gentleman, if it is in order to move it. While on the subject I wish to make one more observation. The Prime Minister was good enough to say on Friday last that I must suffer in my conscience because of having been a party to the contract that was made by the Government of Canada with the Ross Rifle Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If it were so poor a rifle as my hon. friend argued.

I did not argue; I merely stated the facts. I just want to point out, first, that the Ross rifle contract, made in 1902, provided that in case of war or emergency the Government of Canada was at liberty to make or buy rifles where it p'leased and as it pleased, over and above the amount that the Ross Rifle Company could furnish. The second provision that I wish to draw attention to was that the Ross Rifle Company was bound, on du^ notice, to make any alterations demanded by the Government of Canada, and the third provision was that they were bound by the contract to make any other kind of a rifle that the Government of Canada should see fit to *ask or order them to make. So that the original contract provided in these three particulars for the safeguarding by the Government of the interests of the people of Canada under three different sets of circumstances, one of these sets of circumstances being the great condition of war that has arisen. I want to point out further to the Prime Minister and the House that the rifle that was made by the Ross Company under contracts with the Liberal Government was not the rifle that was in the hands of our soldiers in France and Flanders under the administration of this Government.
Was it a good rifle?

I am not sure; it may have been a better rifle. But it was not
the rifle. It could not have been a worse rifle, because the rifle that was put in our ' soldiers' hands in France and Flanders has been taken put of their hands with the consent of this Government forced upon them by the authorities at the British War Office.
What was the rifle that the late Government provided for?

Mark I, Mark II, and
Mark II with three stars. There were three makes provided, and these were all discarded by the present Government. In November, 1911, an order was given for the manufacture of Mark III, and deliveries of that rifle was begun to be made in November, 1912, and it was the Mark III rifle that our soldiers carried in France and Flanders, and which caused the loss of hundreds of lives in those battles.

Before the committee rises at six o'clock, I should like to say just a word with reference to a mutter in which my name was mentioned on Friday last, relative tp the necessity of drawings and specifications for the purpose of the 'manufacture of the new rifle. I have read the debate and observe that the Prime Minister expressed the view that the contract called for drawings and specifications to be served upon the company before the notice would take effect. On the contrary, the situation, although in effect exactly the same, is in direct words this: The drawings and specifications are not referred to in the contract itself as having to be served on the company, but as a practical engineering necessity the specifications and drawings have to be served before there can be a proper contractual relationship between the Government and the company. The Militia Department officials take the ground most positively that there can be in effect and in practice no manufacture of rifleB and no preparation to manufacture rifles until the drawings and specifications are delivered. That is all I desire to say now.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I would submit to
the Government the necessity of clearing the air in regard to the rifle situation. My hon. friend the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has moved an amendment, the purport of which is that the contract which this Government made in Feb-

ruary, 1916, with the Ross Rifle Company should not be fulfilled. What this House and the country is concerned with at the present time is whether or not this country can supply within her own borders a rifle which will be satisfactory to our men when they go out to fight. Without going into anything that has happened in the past, I think it is conceded and declared by hon. gentlemen on both sideis and the proposition is accepted, that the Lee-Enfield pattern, which is now in use in England and which is now being manufactured in England, is such a rifle as would he satisfactory.
I did not catch what the hon. gentleman said. Did he say that the rifle now being manufactured in England is satisfactory?
That is what I understand to be the policy of' the Government, because they have intimated to the Ross Rifle Company that they require that company hereafter to manufacture rifles of that pattern.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: This particular rifle, as I have already explained three or four times, is not being manufactured in England at the present time.

If it is not being
manufactured in England, it is being manufactured for the British Government in the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: For the British1 Government.

The question where
it is being made for the British Government is a matter of no concern to us. The fact is that a certain rifle of a certain pattern is being manufactured and that this Government have adopted that as being the pattern which is satisfactory to them, and have given notice to the Ross Rifle Company to manufacture rifles of that pattern a year from now. The Government, however, have not intimated to the Ross Rifle Company how many rifles will be required, and the whole rifle situation is for the moment obscure on account of the inability of this Government and the company to come to some understanding in regard to it. The Government ought to know how many rifles they require, but they say: We cannot take any further steps until we have a specification; until we have a certain pattern. My right hon. friend will agree with me that any one who has any experience at all in regard to the manufacture in 'Canada and
[Mr. Macdonald.!
elsewhere of goods that are based on steel, especially at this particular juncture, knows that the most important problem is to get the raw material, and if my right hon. friend allows week after week to go by before the blocks of the particular sealed pattern is produced, he is simply postponing to a lengthy, if not to an indefinite period, the manufacture of the rifle by reason of that delay. In. order that material may be obtained, it is necessary that information should be given as to how many rifles the Government will require under their contract. The same thing applies to the stock of the rifle.. All these matters are based on the raw material. Why is it that the Government stand on the brink of this question and do nothing one way or the other? My complaint is this:	They know how many
rifles they will require at the end of the year; they know they will need more than ten thousand, which is the minimum fixed in the contract that they would be bound to take; but yet they decline to indicate how many rifles they require, and it is therefore impossible to obtain material. If three months after this they say they want a hundred thousand rifles of the new pattern, where is the material to come from? My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia takes the position, I understand, that the Ross rifle of the type that was sent to the front, is the best type.

The best in the
world. It has been proved to be so.

That is the position
of the ex-minister in the matter. He is to be commended for the fact that he takes his ground and stands upon it. My hon. friend has had this merit in regard to his administration, that if he * thought a thing was right, he stood by it, no matter what any one in England said about it.

There have been
tests of every kind in connection with the two rifles and the records are available. I challenge the world to produce a record showing that the Ross rifle has come out second to the Lee-Enfield. I do not know whether or not the report of a bogus test has been sent by General Alderson to General Gwatkin. If it has, I propose asking some questions about it. But there has never been an official test, or even a general test, as between the Ross rifle and the Lee-Enfietd rifle wherein the Ross rifle has not in every sense beaten the Lee-Enfield.
While I am on any feet, I desire to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). He said that the

Ross rifle, Mark III, was adopted by the Liberal-Consercative party. I speak frorh memory, but I think it was in 1910 that the [DOT]decision was reached to aldopt the Ross rifle, Mark III.

There is this to be said in favour of the hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) that while he was in charge of the militia at least he had his own opinions and was ready to stand by them. In his correspondence with the Prime Minister he spoke broadly of things that were done, or not done, in England, with regard to the whole administration of affairs in relation to our forces, their supply and equipment:	but when he has the opportunity he does not back up in this House the statements he made.
I have never deviated from any of my statements.

The hon. gentleman wrote these things in a letter to the Prime Minister but has not gbne any further. This whole question of the right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden) or his former Minister of Militia taking acute issue with those who were responsible for certain things done in a military way on the other side of the water, is a very, important problem, and the Ross rifle .question is merely one phase of it. The ex-Minister of Militia was right, or else he was wrong, in certain statements that he made, and makes now, not only in regard to the Ross rifle, but in regard to other supplies paid for by the hard-earned money of the people of Canada and scrapped when they were taken overseas, at a loss of millions and millions. We are asked to accept, without a word, the statement of some gentleman over there because he happens to be connected with the War Office, as though he were an infallible being whose opinion is not to be doubted. The right hon. Prime Minister seems to think that because a man wears the uniform of a British officer he is so far above .anybody who is Canadian bom that by no possibility could anybody in this country venture to question him. The ex-Minister of Militia does not believe in that.

Let me correct my hon. friend. He said "Canadian born." My view of this matter has nothing to do with a man being Canadian born, or British born, or German born. The principle that
I lay down is that a man is in the service of Canada.

The hon. gentleman has interpreted my ideas. We send battalions overseas on the pledge of the ministry that these battalions shall go to the front under their Canadian officers. But when they go across the water, some man who has not worn a. uniform as long as the men under which the Canadian boys are serving tells them that the pledged faith of the Canadian Government matters nothing, but that because he happens to be a British officer those who come from the dominions, no matter what may be their ability and knowledge of their business, shall have nothing to say. And when in this Canadian Parliament we ask the Canadian Minister of Militia to tell us about it, he cannot tell us anything but must cable to London. And for two and a half weeks he has been sending cables to London, and he cannot tell us to-day where we stand in regard to our forces. We are voting $500,000,000, and it is time that we should learn, in the interests of the country, not only in regard to the Ross rifle, but in regard to the status of our men and their equipment, and all other questions overseas, whether this Government is to accept without question the opinions of gentlemen on the other side of the water. We have been in this war almost three years. The casualties of officers and men belonging to the old regiments of Great Britain have been very great indeed. There are men to-day who are commanding regiments going out from Great Britain that have had no longer military experience than the men coming from Canada. Why, then, should we be told that because a man is attached to a Canadian regiment, his opinion about rifles, equipment, or anything else, is worth nothing, as though he belonged to an inferior people whose right to express an opinion is not to be considered?
And who has said that, except it be the hon. gentleman himself?

My hon. friend should know that actions and results speak louder than words. He ought to know that the ex-Minister of Militia has time and time again arraigned the Government, of which he was then a member, for pursuing that policy in Tegard to almost everything in connection with our troops overseas.

Do not a considerable number of Canadian officers hold responsible



positions at the head of the troops in France?

What does the hon. gentleman mean? Is he calling upon us to express exultation and delight because a number of our officers who [DOT] have gone to England are permitted to go to France? If so, he must not expect me to join him. On the other hand, I want to know why it is that two thousand Canadian officers taken from their regiments are not permitted to go to France because somebody who was born in Great Britain, who has had no longer training than many Canadian officers, decides that they shall not go. I want to know why it is that, without regard to the pledged faith of this Government, some man in Great Britain who happened to have a little brief authority decides to butcher our battalions and scatter them to the four winds of heaven. That is what is being done. The reason I mention this matter is because my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) says the Ross rifle is no good-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I did not say the Ross rifle is no good.
The right hon. gentleman says that the Ross rifle is not the weapon that our men ought to be armed with during the war.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I said that it had been exchanged, for reasons which I gave to the House; I did not say what the hon. gentleman said I said; he knows perfectly well that I did not say it.

My right hon. friend is a casuist of the first class. He puts into other words just what I have said. He says the Ross rifle was displaced for good and sufficient reason, that reason being that it w.as not satisfactory to our forces. But the ex-Minister of Militia tells us that it is a better rifle than the Lee-Enfield. The Prime Minister says that because of the opinion they have in England the Ross rifle must be thrown overboard. Well, we have a fully equipped rifle factory in this country. If we cannot make the Ross rifle, why not make some other rifle? We on this side of the House take the position that there is no more reason to believe we cannot make rifles than there was to believe that we could not make shells. When we ask why rifles are not made in this country the right hon. gentleman says: I have given notice of a year-
When was it given?

In	December.
But the Prime Minister does not state how many rifles he wants. He does not pursue the ordinary business policy that a person purchasing manufactured steel would pursue, of indicating his requirements so that those who have to obtain raw material may know what they are to arrange for. And he says that somebody in England does not tell him about the pattern. There is the situation. I think his position proves everything that the ex-Minister of Militia said. That hon. gentleman has told us that for ten months at the beginning of the war he was not permitted to have anything to say. And he predicted that the appointment of an Overseas Minister of Militia would lead to a state of chaos, I think he was a true prophet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have stated the position of the Government over and over again, and I have nothing to add. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) does not understand or appreciate it, that is a matter for himself. I have stated what the difficulties are that the Government will have to consider, and I have nothing to add to what I have already said in that regard.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: What I cannot understand about the situation as explained by the Government is this: Suppose the Government takes the position that they were bound by the contract under ordinary conditions. I do not admit that they were so bound as a matter of fact, but let us assume for the moment that they were bound. But the Government has cancelled other contracts because the condi tions are not ordinary conditions. I believe that under the War Measures Act the Government could take possession of the Ross rifle factory. I believe they could go so far as to make a charge against any one and have him shut up. If the Ross rifle is not right, why is not the manufacture of it stopped? If the Government were to break the contract, what is the worst that could result? The worst would be a merely monetary loss through a successful action for damages for violation of the contract. But, technically, an action could not even be begun against the Government without the Government's own consent. I do not depend upon that however. What I say is that, even admitting the Government's contention, the very worst that could happen would be a suit against them for damages. Well, the Government assumes that our sons ought to be armed with some other

rifle than the Ross rifle. What, then, is the situation? The situation is, that they are putting in the balance on one side a possible monetary loss through a suit for damages and on the other side the proper or improper equipment of our boys, and they are allowing the prospect of monetary loss to outweigh the proper arming of our boys. I cannot see it in any other way. And the manufacture of a rifle is to continue which the Government say cannot be used. We are spending millions of money, and we are going to spend all that is needed for the successful prosecution of this war. I think, to, that Canada will get all the men that have been asked for if the people are properly approached and properly guided. But we must not acquiesce in the idea that anything in the way of a monetary loss by the country or by the manufacturer of these rifles should stand in the way of the boys at the front having the -best rifle that they can get, or that the expenditure of money on a rifle that is not going to be used should be continued. The Finance Minister quite properly delivers lectures on thrift, but how can he reasonably advise ordinary people to stop spending money on things they do not need when he is handing out money for a rifle which he says will not be.used? The answer is: "We have a contract signed." Under the present circumstances that answer is no answer, even if the contract has been signed. Considerations of this kind must be put aside in the face of the great crisis which presents itself. The results of *a proper course of action in this respect might not be welcome to some, but to many families in Canada the results of the present policy will be much more unwelcome than the cancellation of this contract would be. I shall not enter into an argument as to the merits of the rifle. The Government have given their judgment that the rifle is not serviceable; therefore they should at once stop having these rifles manufactured and asking the people to pay for what they are not going to use.
What can the Government do if they want to manufacture the Lee-Enfield rifle, as they say they do? I believe that we ought to have in Canada a concern for the manufacture of an arm for ourselves. No one denies that there is in this country a large equipment and a staff of expert men. I am informed that the British Government are prepared now, and have been for some months, to send over machinery and equipment to the Ross rifle factory for the manufacture of the Lee-Enfield rifle.
31i
The duty of the Government is plain. No matter what the monetary consequences -may be, stop manufacturing a rifle that you do not purpose using, take advantage of the offer of the British Government, bring over machinery and equipment and begin at once to manufacture a rifle which the experts of this Government say is the one that our men at the front should use. The necessity of winning the war is paramount to everything else, and, if it cannot be done through an arrangement with Sir Charles Ross, I would go so far as to say that we should nationalize the Ross rifle concern, take advantage of the offer of the British Government and proceed at once to manufacture g, rifle whieh we can use.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has worked himself up into a state of excitement-
I am in earnest, not excited.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: -upon a suggestion which, if he had stopped for a moment to think, he would not have made. He is speaking of the manufacture of these rifles in connection with the arm which is used by the Canadian forces at the front. I have explained at least half a dozen times since this debate began that the Canadian Expeditionary Forces at the front are supplied with the Lee-Enfield rifle and that the British Government have entered into a definite engagement to that end. When my hon. friend, therefore, introduces the bogie of the Canadian forces at the front being supplied with Ross rifles which are to be paid for out of this vote, he introduces a suggestion which, if he had paid any attention to the debate, he would have known to be of no relevancy whatever.
The rifles, then, are not going to be used?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The rifles will be used for certain purposes, just as the Ross rifles, which are being supplied to the British Government under their order will be used for certain purposes.

Will they be used for
war or for peace purposes?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
They will be used in the training of our men, and they may, as I have said already, be used in warfare under different conditions. There is a difference of opinion about the merits of the Ross rifle. I have never ventured an opinion on the merits of the rifle, because I do not

possess sufficient knowledge and experience in such matters to make my opinion of any value. I have to go, therefore, by the opinions of others who have the requisite knowledge and experience in this respect. The member for South Renfrew seems to be under the impression that it would be merely a question of paying an amount equal to the profits on the manufacture of the rifle, or something of that kind, if we cancelled this contract at once. In the contract as made by the Government of which the hon. member of South Renfrew was 'a Jmeimber, no authority was reserved for cancelling it. If we should say to the Ross Rifle Company: "We will not accept your rifles," what would be the result? The material for those rifles has been obtained, and the parts have very largely been constructed. The parts have not yet been assembled, but if I mistake not very little will remain to be done after March 31 except the assembling. The result of such a proposal as that made by my hon. friend, therefore, would be that we would have to pay for these 80,000 rifles and would not get them for any purposes for which they might be found useful. I should not suppose that 'any person possessing ordinary common sense would suggest that 'this be done.
Neither would I.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is precisely, what my hon. friend suggests, if he i aware of the facts.
Not at 9*11.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What does he
suggest, then?
I have suggested it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If the hon.
gentleman's suggestion means anything at all, it means precisely what I have stated.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman either was not very sincere in his remarks

which of course, I do not suggest, or, he did not understand what he was talking about.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I venture to say that the hon. gentleman did not know the extent to which the manufacture of these rifles has proceeded, in the production of the various parts which will eventually be assembled into the completed rifle. If we took the course which he suggests, the net result would be that we would pay for the riflles, but would not get them.

I am not going to take any part in the discussion of this contract. I have -not interfered in any orders in connection with the Ross rifle practically since the war began, because both political parties in days gone by have yielded to improper influences in seeking to make a political football of the manufacture of the Ross rifle under the inspiration of interested parties across the water. In our experience in South Africa we found that the Lee-Ehfield rifle jammed repeatedly. I did not want to take up this line of argument, but I purpoise doing it owing to the trend that the discussion has taken. I say that the Lee-Enfield rifle jammed repeatedly in South Africa. I can point you to the records of the British House of Commons which show that British officers said that to put that rifle in the hands of their soldiers in South Africa was murdering them. More of their own men, they said, were injured by the Lee-Enfield rifle, owing to the defects of it, than were injured by the Boer Mauser rifle.
The British experience in South Africa was that, again and again, not only did the Lee-Enfield jam, but it burst. We all had that experience in South Africa. Then it was found in South Africa that the bolts dropped out very readily. We have had none of that with the Ross rifle. The Lee-Enfield rifle in South Africa was very badly sighted; some of the rifles fired to the left, some fired to the right. Towards the close of the war we got some of them to fire accurately, but the sighting of the rifle was very bad. So we had seven or eight very serious objections to the Lee-Enfield rifle in South Africa. As a result of that the British Government purposed changing their rifle. The British Lee-Enfield private arsenals unfortunately were owned, and are owned to-day, by German interests. I make that statement without fear of contradiction-
A serious statement.

The stock may have been transferred, but they were owned by German authorities, who fought and opposed any change in the British rifle, planning for this war. When this matter was realized, it was decided by the Canadian Government to take up a new rifle. The Mannlicher, a long, quick-firing rifle, was used extensively by the Boers in South Africa. It was not of as long range as the Mauser or the Lee-Enfield, but it was an excellent rapid-fire gun. It was a straight pull rifle the same as the Ross, only with a

different mechanism. It was an excellent rifle for any range short of 800 yards, up to close quarters, and we learned to our cost what that rapid-fire rifle meant in South Africa, Accordingly I have yet to see the man who knew anything about a rifle-and there are a great many people making motions about rifles here who do not know the butt end of a rifle from the muzzle-
Is the British War Office aware that the Lee-Enfield is controlled and owned by German firms?
I said the private factories. The British factories make the Lee-Enfield, but there are also private factories that make the Lee-Enfield.
Have they received any orders during the war?
I presume they are turning them out right along. The stock, previous to the war, was held by German interests, and that was known in England; I presume that the British authorities knew of it.
Does the hon. member suggest that General French or General Haig is in league with Germans?
Neither has said a word against the Ross rifle.
The hon. gentleman cannot read.	.
Oh yes, I can.
Then you cannot understand.	x

Oh, yes, I can understand, but my hon. friend is so thick in the head that he cannot understand. There is not a word in any report from General Haig or General French saying that the Ross is inferior to the Lee-Enfield or that there has ever been a comparative test.
What about General Alderson, does he understand rifles?
I do not think he would know the butt from the muzzle.
What rifles are the Canadians using in France?
The Lee-Enfield at present.
The Lee-Enfield?

Yes, the Lee-Enfield, I am very sorry to say. The whole mistake in this matter was this; when the
Canadians were sent over we armed them with Ross rifles, and when any attempt was made to change anything, the British authorities should have been told:	These
are Canadian troops; that is made in Canada, we have equipped these men in this way, and it is none of your business; we are responsible for wihat these men carry and what these men do and we are willing to assume the responsibility. If we had done that and told these gentlemen to keep their hands off, the thing would have been all right. I understand there has been a report read, containing the answer to the ten questions. Suggestions were sent around for weeks by somebody's inspiration, little printed slips were sent around to our troops asking questions about the Ross rifle. These men, having experience of the retreat, the horrible retreat, the murderous retreat of the British soldiers, from Mons to the Marne, where thousands and tens of thousands went down, as the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) might say, murdered, not by the Lee-Enfield rifle, but by the British ammunition-three factories turned out bad ammunition that jammed the rifles. That was the Lee-Enfield rifle; there was not a Ross rifle on the continent at that time. The Lee-Enfield rifle jammed over and over and over again. The Munsters were shot to pieces, the Gordons and the Guards were shot to pieces by the jamming of rifles with bad ammunition. And yet this gentleman from Edmonton, with the opportunity of getting at these facte, stands up and blames the jamming on the Ross rifle.
What rifle had the Canadians when they were shot to pieces?
They had bad ammunition, that is what they had,

That is not what Sir
Douglas Haig said.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, that is what he says.
No it is not.

I happen to know. These ten questions were sent around week after week. The boys, most of them, had been accustomed to the Lee-Enfield, and any new rifle coming in, to which they were not accustomed, would naturally be a little edd to them. I quite well remember that when the Snider-Enfield rifle gave place to the Martini, there was any amount of objection. The boys wanted to stick to the Snider-
COMMOiNS
Enfield. So when the Lee-Enfield came in and took the place of the Martini, the boys wanted to stick to the Martini. So when the Lee-Enfield in turn gave place to the Ross, a number of the soldiers were afraid that the bolt would blow back; they did not understand the mechanism and naturally objected to the straight pull. One of these questions was:	Do you not find the
Rose rifle a little heavy? The Ross' rifle with bayonet is of the .same weight as the Lee-Enfield with bayonet. Another question was: Don't you find the Ro.se rifle too short in. the bayonet? The .idea there was that the other fellow would get at him in using the bayonet, forgetting that a long rifle with a long bayonet is far easier to thrust aside than a short rifle with a short bayonet. Why I saw Henry Godwin, with a little dagger, beat the champion of the British Army with rifle and bayonet. It is not the length of the rifle and bayonet but the way it is handled; and then, too, the leverage that can be exerted on the end of a long rifle and bayonet by an opponent is much greater than in the case of a short rifle and bayonet, so that the long rifle and bayonet can be more easily thrust aside and is so less useful in the attack. These questions were sent around and there is not one of them that could not be answered in favour of the Ross rifle. General French never had a comparative test. I asked .him to have an official, test of the two riflesi, I offered to let him pick his best experts in England and I would pick the best experts in the Canadian Army, and if I did mot trim him to a finish on every point I would agree to swallow the two rifles-a rather difficult job to perform. We have had a lot o,f talk and nonsense about this thing and therefore I want it clearly understood, in reading these ten question, that not one of them is borne out by any comparative test ever produced in France.
I challenge the Prime Minister to produce a solitary comparative test-he cannot do it, because I have gone into this and fought it out. It is like many another thing. For instance, why did we pay $5,240 for trucks when our own better ones are now running while these aTe in the ditch, and ours could have been had for $2,800? Because I bowed, foolishly bowed-I should have resigned from the Cabinet or forced the issue of our being allowed to run our own show. Then why was our: Oliver equipment discarded? I passed through with the Prime Minister and we only saw two or three regiments, apart from the Canadians, equipped wdth 
the Webb equipment. I saw more Canadians with Webb equipment than British soldiers. This is the way this humbug goes on. up and down. The inspection and throwing out of our material has ibeen simply, to my mind, a scandal. We had another report-T wonder if that was read? Was that report from General Alderson to General Gwatkin read? Has the Prime Minister ever made any inquiry as to where that report came from?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: How it got out?
Yes. To whom did General Gwatkin hand that report?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I asked about
that and I understood it got out without his authority or knowledge. I do not know how.

Then why was
General Gwatkin not dismissed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend was responsible for it.

Oh, no, pardon me, I was not responsible for it. If I had been he would have gone long ago, and the Prime Minister knows it. With regard to this report of Alderson's, Sir Max Aitken and General Carson told me that defective ammunition was being issued. This was after the affair, to which I referred the other evening, concerning the 28th Battalion under Colonel Embury.
Where did the defective ammunition come from?

There were three
brands of it. I think two were British and one was from the United States '>ui r one was Canadian. I want to say tout none of our ammunition turned out bad. I forget the names of the brands.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They -ire ail on record.

Yes, they are on record. The three brands were defective and no rifle could have fired them. One of them was so deadly that to have sent men to the firing line with it would have been simply murder. We found an ordnance officer attached to Canadian headquarters issuing that ammunition to the extent of
5,000	rounds which were placed in the pouches of one battalion which was in the blow-up. I have no hesitation in saying that that ordnance officer should have been led out and shot, and if I had been Tunning the show I would have carried that out. I

protested, and demanded Ms dismissal, but he is there yet, I understand.
What happened at St. Julien?

At St. Jnlien, the Ross rifle was.nsed. The only real rifle victory in this "war was fought and won by the Ross rifle, and half of the boys were using bad ammunition at that.
About this Alderson or -Gwatkin report- I want the Prime Minister to take note of this, and perhaps Gwatkin will get a ticket for home next week-that report was based on a test between two boys to show that it was bad ammunition. Following upon the Embury affair, General Aider-son sent Sir Max Aitken and General Carson each a copy of the report. Each off his own hat wrote him that the report was false, that no such test had ever 'been held, that it was only a test of ammunition and not of the rifle. One of them pointed out to me moreover that one of the boys who took part in the test, a boy from Millbrook, had never fired a rifle 50 times, in his lifetime. He was driving a motor engine and was picked out to test the defective cartridges. When an officer who understood the use of a rifle took it, the test showed that the Lee-En-field rifle jammed far more frequently than the Ross rifle. They wired to General Alderson, and one of them wrote and sent a corrected report, .and yet General Gwatkin did not hand that report out with the other, although, as a matter of fact, it oame on the same mail. No explanation was given to the House, and the .correcting report was [DOT]not given out to the press at the same time as the other. There is no doubt that the world put two and two together. Nobody could know of the conspiracy in one of my departments, and this was part 'and parcel of the conspiracy from start to finish. And yet these gentlemen .are there to-day.
There is another matter to which I would refer. The Princess Patricia's battalion went to the front carrying the Lee-Enfield rifle. They were cut to pieces through their rifles jamming. I have letters from the late Colonel Farquhar telling me about it. At that time they had not discovered that the jamming was due to bad ammunition, and he thought it was due to the dirt. He wrote saying " Fix all the boys up with oilcloths, and tell them to take the bolt out, and wipe it clean with the oilcloth," -because he said the rifles jammed over and over again with the dirt. A young fellow, a captain from Calgary, told me & week or two ago that
when he was in the firing line-he was then a private

they carried sticks and the staves of barrels so as to smash open the bolts in their rifles, which were Lee-Enfields, when they jammed. We did not hear anything of this because there w.as no one interested in decrying the Lee-Enfield rifle. I would not decry it now but for the course taken by certain gentlemen in this House. The Lee-Enfield was found defective in South Africa; it was rejected by the Japanese Government eighteen years ago as being absolutely unfit for service. It was unfit for service then and it is unfit to-day compared with the Ross rifle. The chamber of the Ross rifle was found to be slightly smaller, and we enlarged it, -and every possible objection to the rifle was removed thereby.
There is another matter that I desire to bring up while I am on my feet-I did not intend speaking on this question at all. I have received several cablegrams from officers of certain battalions at the front in the firing line stating that their battalions are going to be broken up to make way for certain other battalions. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has referred to the Highland Brigade of Nova Scotia being broken up. The Prime Minister will recollect that when Nova Scotia sent its first battalion-it was really only half a battalion-the boys were splendid; there were none finer in the world, but that the men did not reflect the credit on the province that they should have done because they did not go into the firing line as a battalion, but were kept as reserves. Individually, they were magnificent, but they did not have the opportunity of doing credit to the province that they would have liked to have had. When the Highland Brigade of Nova Scotia was organized I felt a little keen in regard to the matter because of what had happened, and I took the matter up with the Prime Minister. With his authority I gave my solemn pledge to the officers of the brigade and to the committee that had helped to organize it, that it would be kept intact. The Prime Minister may recall that on one occasion he spoke to me -about the 85th Battalion. I said, "For heaven's sake, let us carry out one pledge we have made to the people of Nova Scotia." I merely recall that to the Prime Minister. I gave the same pledge to the Irish Battalion of Montreal. We had Scotch Battalions, English Battalions, Canadian Battalions and darkie battalions, and when the Irishmen of Montreal got their battalion together I thought it was only just to give them the

promise and to carry it out, that they would go as a regiment to the front. I did the same with the I04th Battalion of New Brunswick. Every one who knows our history will remember that in 1812 the old 104th marched *all through to Canada, as it was >at that time, through the wilds in a Canadian winter. When the 104th Battalion was organized for this war we gave the people of New Brunswick to understand that that regiment would be held intact. The same held good of the 105th Battalion from Prince Edward Island. These were the regiments that were to. 'be held intact. That was the plan, and I have seen and heard nothing to cause me to deviate from it to-day.
I -may point out that Camp Borden trained more men during the past summer than there are training in England to-day, that Camp Hughes, in Manitoba, trained more men during the past summer than are m England training to-day, and that Valear-tier and other camps have trained almost as many, and yet we do not find a resident Minister of Militia at Camp Borden, at Camp Hughes, or at Camp Valcartier. Why all this paraphernalia should be introduced in London, I have never (been able to find out. General Carson, with Colonel George Murphy, and thirty-one assistants, ran the business, and when' any hon. gentleman asked for any news of his friends at the front he got an answer within a few days. When any hon, gentleman asked if any one was wounded or wanted a report about any one, he got his answer in a very few days from General Carson. To-day you get nothing. General Carson with only thirty-one officers could keep the work going, train men, and send them to the front and win battles, whereas to-day I am told there are 700 assistants, costing $6,000,000 a year, as the result of the action of the Minister of Finance when he ordered the Prime Minister to appoint an Overseas Minister; I forget what he was going to do. We find all that saddled on the country, and I presume to-night the Minister of Finance is preaching thrift and economy to the people of Ottawa.
My plan, and I want it emphasized, and I want the Prime Minister to consider it, was this: We have four divisions at the front. Now I cannot see why we should not have six or even eight, if we have plenty of men in England, and if they are well looked after. I would not run all the new divisions in fresh, but I would do so gradually, after the boys have got in

harness and been trained. We need not hold any more of the front than now, but this plan would always allow us to have two divisions in rest. It would absorb the Nova Scotia Highland Brigade, the Quebec Brigade, including tfie Irish Begiment, the regiments from the eastern townships, the French Canadian regiments, the New Brunswick Brigade, and regiments from the West. Every corps would then have its local representation from all over the Dominion, not necessarily battalion units, because battalions from most localities are now broken up, but taking five or eight battalions from Ontario we could have one part of them as the active brigade, and the other part could be kept in training for details. I worked out the plan with the War Office, with Sir Douglas Haig, and Sir William Bobertson, and it met with the approval of every one of them, and for the life of me I cannot see why the plan has not been carried out. This plan would obviate the necessity of breaking up the Nova Scotia Highland Brigade, the New Brunswick Brigade, the Prince Edward Island Battalion, the Irish Begiment of Montreal, the Quebec Battalion and others, and there would be no trouble whatever. Then in the spring, if a drive comes, instead of having four divisions we should have six divisions trained during the winter months, and they would be ready for any drive that might come along. Our losses with the six divisions would be no more than with the four, because we should be holding no more of the front. Our losses would be less per brigade, although the total might be the same.
I might point out that if it had been distinctly understood there was to be no monkeying with the Boss rifle, no changes at all, there would not have been one word more about it. Let me point out further, in regard to Sir John French's report-and I do not blame Sir John French for that report, for it was concocted by the same people who sent over these other reports. I do not blame Sir John French for the statements he made, for he only accepted the statements of Alderson, and the report was made up for Alderson by some of these whippersnappers who have been mentioned, and who knew nothing of a rifle, and whose only ambition was to get rid of everything of Canadian make. Sir John French says in his report that he found 3,000 Lee-En-fields already in the division. I told Sir John French that the British regulars would come along at night, when they did not

have an opportunity in the day time, and steal the Ross ride for their snipers and sharpshooters. The British regulars soon realized the deadly value of the Ross rifle for that kind of work. In the morning our fellows would find their Ross rifles gone and Lee-Enfields left in their stead.
I did not intend to say anything about this matter, but was prompted to do so by the trend given to the debate by some hon. gentleman recalling the old days when some hon.-gentlemen who did not belong to the Liberal persuatiom attacked the Rose rifle. It strikes me that it is not well for the Ross rifle or for the welfare of the troops that this criticism has been launched. The only trouble with the Ross rifle has been bad ammunition. The Lee-Enfields have jammed over and over again. The Ross rifle has jammed over and over again with bad ammunition, but it has not jammed nearly so badly as the Lee-Enfield has jammed.

I should like to say a word before the motion is put. We have just listened to a very serious charge by the ex-Minister of Militia against not only this Government but the British Government as well. He says that the Lee-En-field is no good now, and that it was no good at the time of the South African war. What must we think of this Government and the British Government if the statements made by the ex-Minister of Militia are true? He takes the position that he knows all about the merits of the Ross rifle, and that the chief military authorities in Great Britain and all the members of the British Government know absolutely nothing whatever about it, and he says that the Leo-Enfield rifle is not a fit weapon to put into the hands of our soldiers, let alone the British soldiers. That is a very serious charge to make, and I think some one on the Government benches should have something to say about it. I will not go any further into that; it is a matter for the Government to deal with, and surely the British Government might take notice of it too. If, then, the Ross rifle is declared to be no good by one who claims to know everything about it-
I said the ammunition was no good. I did not say the rifle was no good.

He said that the Lee-Enfield was no good in South Africa and no good in the present war, and that on every occasion -when a test was made the
Ross rifle proved superior to the Lee-En-field. The ex-minister will not deny that.
Hear, hear.

He has the courage of his convictions, and is not afraid to stand by them on the floor of Parliament. While I cannot agree with the ex-minister, I certainly admire his courage in standing by what he believes to be true. My hon. friend does not say that it was bad ammunition. He says the Lee-Enfield was not a good rifle.
I said that in this war neither the Ross rifle nor the Lee-Enfield had jammed with good ammunition.
I accept my hon. friend's explanation.
It is not an explanation; it is my statement.

There are one or two things that seem to stand out in the strong light of day in connection with the Ross rifle. Efforts have been made by the Government to show that they were bound to accept the Ross rifle under the contract made by the late Government. But the contract did not provide that the rifle had to be the Ross rifle. The company had to furnish any rifle the Government approved of, and the Government had the right at any time to change the specifications of the Ross rifle that was being manufactured for them. No matter what is said to the contrary, this Government is absolutely responsible for the Ross rifle that is being put in the hands of our Canadian soldiers. I am not going to hold the Government responsible for what happened before the war. There is no question that the Ross rifle is a good target rifle, and probably one of the best sporting rifles in the world, but soon after the war started, as soon as our Canadian troops were engaged in the spring of 1915, it was demonstrated that the Ross rifle was an absolutely unsuitable weapon for our soldiers in the trenches. That is the report of everybody.
When was that demonstrated?
In the spring of 1915.
Before that it had not been demonstrated.

I say that it was demonstrated in the first battles in which the Canadian soldiers used the Ross rifle. I know that in the spring of 1915 the British authorities in the field re-armed the First

Division with the Lee-Enfield rifle. Previous to- that time word was coming hack every -day of the week from the Canadian soldiers at the front that the Boss rifle was absolutely unsatisfactory, and that on every occasion where it was possible for a Canadian soldier to throw away his Ross rifle and pick up a Lee-Enfield, he did so. Now, dp you think that the Canadian soldiers in the First Division, our own people were all crazy; that they were led astray by the manufacturers of the Lee-Enfield rifle in Great Britain; that these men who were fighting and giving their lives for their country did not know one rifle from the another, -did not know whether the Ross rifle was a good one or a poor one?
Might I point out to my hon. friend that it was not until October, 1915, that the Canadians seemed to realize that bad ammunition was the cause of the trouble?

Then all I have to say is that the British war authorities took action a long time before the Canadian soldiers found out that the Ross rifle was not a satisfactory rifle, because Sn the spring of 1915 the First Division was rearmed with Lee-Enfield rifles. I hold the Government responsible vfrom that time forward. I do not hold the Government responsible up to that time; but when, in the spring of 1915, now almost two years ago, they got word that the Ross rifle was an unsatisfactory war weapon-and they got that information from the men carrying the rifles and also from the British authorities-

Is the Government to be condemned for not observing the British regulations? The British authorities threw out the trucks for the First Division, and then, for the Second Division, I refused to have the trucks changed.

That is a matter in regard to which the ex-Minister of Militia and the Prime Minister of Canada are at daggers drawn, the Prime Minister of Canada can deal with that question. I have seen a good deal of correspondence between my hon. friend and the Prime Minister and I am free to admit that the ex-Minister of Militia got the best of that correspondence.

And I will gat the best too when it comes to a comparison between the Ross rifle and the Lee-Enfield rifle.

'Mr. TURRIFF: If my hon. friend can do that, he is a better man than I think he is, because it does not seem reasonable to me that the British Government, the war ministers, and the generals of Great Britain who are fighting in the fields of France and Flanders to-day can all be fooled or bribed by the Germans. I do not believe that for one moment, and I do not believe the people of Canada or the people of Great Britain will take the view of the ex-Minister of Militia as against that of the British Government, the war generals and the Government of Canada.
'Sir SAM HUGHES:	May I point this
out to my hon. friend? I do not suppose one out of a hundred thousand ever heard anything about the matter. It has been, shown that reports are allowed to pass through without eveT being read.
What changes did the hon. gentleman say we should have made that were suggested by the Ross Rifle Company?

Does my hon. friend
say that no changes were ever suggested by the Ross Rifle Company?

I do not know what
the hon. gentleman refers to? He siays that the Ross Rifle Company suggested changes which we should have made. When he says that, he O'Ught to know what the changes are; and if he knows what they are, he ought to tell us.

I ask my hon. friend,
who is a member of the Government: Were changes ever suggested by the Ross Rifle Company?

I am sorry I cannot
answer. I do not know what the hon. gentleman is driving at. When I make a statement I will give the evidence in support of it. I am asking the hon. gentleman to give the evidence in support of his statement.

If my hon. friend, who is a member of the Government, cannot answer, how does he expect me, a private
meniber, to answer? My hon. friend will not make the statement, and I challenge him to make the statement. He has made the statement that the Government was bound by the contract made by the late Government, and he has not vet substantiated that statement. If he can do so, we would like to hear him; but my hon. friend has taken good care not to make the statement that no changes were ever suggested by the company manufacturing the Ross rifle. My hon. friend has not made that statement, and I do not think he purposes making it, because he knows he will be getting into deep water if ihe does. In May or June of last year the British Government said: Don't .send over any more Ross rifles.
Did the Ross Rifle Company suggest to the Government that any changes should be made in the rifle, and if so, what changes?

Now, my hon. friend is trying to take upon himself the duties of the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen). We all give the Solicitor General credit for being very clever, and able, and sharp, and I think that if he did not make much progress it would be unwise for the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) to try. Last spring the British Government said: Don't Send over any more Ross rifles. The Ross rifle is the one that had been in the" hands of our Canadian boys at the front. I have heard men who have been in the trenches, and have been fortunate enough to come back, say that in hundreds of cases our Canadian boys have stood with their Ross rifles, jammed and useless in their hands and the Germans have come up and shot them in their tracks. I say again, the Government is responsible to a very large extent for much of the loss of life that occurred through the Canadian soldiers being armed with the Ross rifle long after the Government knew that that rifle was unsatisfactory as a war weapon. We have information, I do not know how true, that a number of Ross rifles-we are told, tens of thousands of them-were tampered with in an effort to improve them, by men either at the front or in Great Britain; that the bolt was taken out and tempered, and was so hardened that it became as brittle as glass, so that in many cases the little knob that keeps the bolt from flying out broke off like a piece of glass and the rifle became useless after firing a few shots. That was done under the regime of the Prime

Minister, and we have never heard of any punishment being meted out to the men who tampered with that rifle. Yet these rifles were put into the hands of our soldiers without being tested, after this tempering of the bolt had been done. Who is responsible? Is it the Prime Minister, or is it the ex-Minister of Militia? That mistake cost the lives of hundreds of Canadian boys.

I might point out that the hon. gentleman is wrong. These rifles were put into the hands of soldiers, training in camp in England, and the tempering or tampering, was detected. Those rifles never got to the front.

I understand that this
tempering was done in England.

Let us explain.
After the tempering had been done the rifles were put into the hands of soldiers to be used, and the aiscovery of the defects was made in England before the troops crossed.
On whose authority was that tempering done?

I never got to the
bottom of it. It was only last year that it occurred, and it is one of the things I was working at when I came home.

At all events, it appears that authority was given by somebody to do this tempering, and these rifles were put into the hands of our boys, and hundreds of them lost their lives on account of the rifle proving useless. Not having proper inspection they-
Sir SAM HUGHES. Let me correct the hon. gentleman. Not one of the rifles with a bad bolt got to the front. It is not true what the hon. gentleman says about our boys losing their lives through this-perfect nonsense. If the rifle jammed, it was due to bad ammunition and not to the rifle itself. I examined the matter critically and am confident that that is the case. What harm would happen if the knob of the bolt broke off? If the weapon was defective, the man had only to pick up another one. But this tempering was done in England. As soon as I heard of it, I ordered an inquiry, and this was under way when I came home.
When was this?
Last ye-r.

Here we have the statement that this was done apparently without the knowledge or authority of the Minister of Militia of that day. Was it

done behind his back by his collegues- or was it done by somebody in the Old Country? My opinion is that many of those rifles, thousands of them, got across to France and Belgium, and in the time of battle they proved useless after the first few shots. I have talked with returned soldiers, and officers too. The ex-Minister of Militia said that what I have said is absurd-that any man lost his life through the rifle jamming. I have heard these men say that they have seen scores of men shot down with rifles in their hands they could not use.
Due to bad aoiuni-tion.
Well, there is the position of affairs. And in the face of all this the Prime Minister asks this Committee to vote $2,666,000 to buy more Ross rifles.
I challenge the hon. gentleman to give the name of an officer who has seen a score of men shot down.

I have their word for it, and I would take the word of an officer who has been in battle as quickly as I would take the word of the ex-Minister of Militia. I have been told not only by officers but by men that these things have occurred. Why has the rifle been changed? We are asked to vote the money for the manufacture of 80,000 additional Ross rifles, a 'large number already delivered, and a large number not yet delivered nor even manufactured. Surely the time for the Government to cancel the contract for the Ross rifle was when the British Government sent word that they did not want any more Ross rifles sent to Great Britain, and that they would arm the Canadian soldiers with Lee-Enfields. Surely that was the time to let the matter stand in abeyance until the necessary machinery could be put in to manufacture the Lee-Enfield or any other rifle that the Government decided upon. But my hon. friends did not take that means of getting a good rifle to put into the hands of the soldiers; in spite of the advice of the British Government, they continued to manufacture the Ross rifle. My right hon. friend now asks for $2,666,000 to manufacture a rifle which, generally speaking, will not be used for war purposes, but will be utilized for training the men in Great Britain. But it is not necessary to pay $28 for a dummy rifle with which the soldiers may drill and learn how to handle a rifle. You could get something to take the place of a rifle for drilling purposes at a

cost of $1, or, at the most $2. My right hon. friend, however, purposes spending $2,666,000 for a rifle which will not be used in war except under certain circumstances; which is not going to be sent to France or Belgium, where the fighting is going on- and he is going to continue purchasing this rifle for months to come. This is an absurd position for the Government to take, and the people will hold the Government responsible, not only for the kind of rifle that they have put into the hands of the soldiers, but also for the waste of money in purchasing rifles that are not going to be used. It is such a waste of money that the only thing that I can compare it with is the extravagance of this Government in everything connected with the war.

Mr. Chairman, the Government is in the position to-night of being attacked from the opposite side of the House because we authorized the substitution of Lee-En-field rifles for the Ross rifles too late, and as a result are blamable before the people of Canada-and, at the same time we are attacked by the ex-Minister of Militia because we authorized this substitution too soon. It is rather amusing to observe the efforts of hon. gentlemen opposite making their attack from one viewpoint with all the vigour in their power, watching the exMinister of Militia making his attack from the opposite viewpoint with the vigour that he is capable of, and at the same time struggling desperately to keep on sympathetic terms with the ex-Minister of Militia. I desire to assure the committee that between the two the members of the Government feel quite comfortable in the belief that the entire course pursued by the Administration with regard to rifles has been the right course; that the substitution was made at the right time, not too soon not too late, made at the only time when in the eyes of intelligent and impartial men we could justify it to the people of Canada.
I would not undertake on any occasion to discuss the comparative merits of the two rifles; no one is less capable of that discussion than I. We cannot be governed as members of the Administration by our own views of the comparative merits of the rifles; we must be governed by the views of those whose opinions are entitled to be the controlling factor in the decision of such a vital question. We have been governed by the views of those men; we have followed their views and the results have justified our decision.
If I may be allowed to make one remark as to what principle I think .should be followed an the matter of the selection of a .standard rifle for Canada it would be that we .should use the same rifle as is adopted as thte result of experience by Great Britain herself; that our rifle should be the same rifle as hers, and that the combined wisdom of the two countries should be at the back of whatever rifle is used. That has not been the case in Canada for many years, and those responsible for that not being the case are the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite. They are the persons who, in 1902, undertook to establish a standard service arm for this country; who pinned the fate of this country in peace and war to that arm, and who did so in defiance of the judgment of the authorities in Great Britain. The Liberal Government of Canada entered into a contract on March 27, 1902, for the production of a rifle, in Canada of which they were to supply a standard sample to the Ross Rifle Company. They later established .a factory on the hill at Quebec and they made that selection in defiance of the advice of the officer commanding the troops in Canada, who informed them that in his judgment it was by no means a suitable place for the establishment of a rifle factory. Political considerations seemed to have governed them from the first, while military considerations were left altogether in the background. Before they went ahead they received a protest from the War Office of Great Britain against the adoption in this or in any part of the British Empire of a standard rifle differing from the standard rifle adopted by Great Britain herself. In defiance of that protest they went ahead, adopted a standard	rifle,	the	Ross rifle, Mark I, ,placed it	with	the Ross	rifle Company, and manufactured that rifle for some years. They .are the parties responsible for the adoption of that standard and for all the consequences that necessarily ensued, And, what consequences necessarily ensued? What consequences are attributable to the action of those who adopted this as the standard rifle of Canada?They later altered the type in some respects, maintaining the main principle, and they	called that	the Ross	rifle MarkII.	Later	they	altered it	again and
they called that the Ross rifle Mark II ***, and that was the rifle adopted by the late Government until shortly before they went out of office.

The hon. member for Edmonton (Hon. Frank Oliver) speaking, I know, not intentionally in the wrong, but utilizing an article which appeared about a month ago in the Toronto Globe, made himself responsible for the assertion that it was this Government which changed from the Mark II to the Mark III rifle.
Hear, hear.

He adheres to that still; he still Slings to the Globe article of January 6 last, scarcely a line of which could be properly described as anything less than loathesome mendacity. I purpose establishing what I say. I do not think that the hon. member for Edmonton even yet intends to make a statement that is wrong.
He does not.

He does not? I happen to have the order in council here, right in front of me, which was passed by the late Administration, adopting the Mark III rifle. No more suitable time than now is likely to present itself for reading that. It is dated October 2, 1911. For the purpose of fitting the story to the necessity of the argument, the Globe has dated it in November, 1911; but, unfortunately for the Globe, the order in council is dated October 2, 1911. Undoubtedly, I made the same statement, and I made it in Montreal also. Certainly, if we had power, we would have done it and paid the damages rather than put an inferior weapon into the hands of our troops, if we had available a better weapon. But would the hon. gentleman even hint that on that account we were not bound by the contract? Of course we -were bound by the contract.
Bound by a contract which you could easily put an end to?
The same as any other contract. If we were not bound by that contract, no government and no individual ever was bound by any.
Will the minister allow me to ask him a question?
Yes.
Did the contract with the Ross Rifle Company bind the Government to the making of an inefficient rifle?
Does the hon. gentleman consider that a question?
Yes. Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to answer it?

It bound the Government to every term of the contract-and that is what I asserted in Montreal. Nobody would for a moment suggest that we would make'an inefficient rifle if we could make a better one and put it in the hands of our troops in time.
What I am asking the minister is this: did the contract bind the Government to compel the Ross Rifle Company to make an inefficient rifle?
The hon. member for ' Edmonton knows-I am sorry to say it to him, because I have respect for him that his question is simply nonsense.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.
The contract speaks for itself, and to its terms we were bound.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon; I asked him a fair question. I ask him now either for a fair answer or a civil refusal.

It binds us to make the rifle that for the time being is the standard rifle. No government in the world would make that standard rifle a day longer than it could help, no matter what the damages were, if they could make a better rifle and get it to the troops in time.
Does not the contract permit the Government to change the form of the rifle at its pleasure?
With a year's notice.
