Have changes not been made by the Ross Rifle Company since the beginning of the war on one month s or two months' notice?
Mr. MEIGHEN- Trifling changes, like the weight of a nose band or something like that-never a change in the type. The hon. member for Carleton stated that he would take the word of the man who runs the factory, irrespective altogether of other authorities. He made that statement in the House, and I have it before me. Let me on this occasion, without at all reflecting on the ability of Sir Charles Ross or the good faith of his company, say this: there was an order once before to change the type of the rifle. A year is all that is allowed by the contract within which to make such a change. What time was taken the last time the type of the rifle was changed? Notice was served op the company on December 28, 1910, and the first rifles of the new pattern were delivered in November, 1912, nearly, 23 months afterwards. Something intervened-I am not saying it was the fault of the company. They in the meantime produced some other rifles; they kept their hands busy. But you cannot always depend upon prognostications, particularly on the part of men whose enthusiasm for the rifle, and, perhaps, for their factory, honestly influences their judgment. The hon. member for Carleton observed that the Prime Minister had quoted the authority of a letter signed by Sir George Perley that in the opinion of, as he decribed it, " some official " over in England, that factory could not produce rifles of a new pattern in quantities within two years. Not only was a year necessary, but in the judgment of " some official," to use the graphic language of the hon. member for Carleton, two years were necessary. He said we were taking the judgment of " some _ official " instead of the judgment of the man who owned the factory. Well, as the Prime Minister pointed out, we are doing nothing of the kind, we are taking all, and making the best decision that we can. But who is this "some official"? He was the Minister of Munitions of the British Government qf that day. The Minister of Munitions of the British Government was referred to as " some official," and the hon. member for Carleton said that in his judgment this " some official " was incompetent and that the Primp Minister should be severely castigated for listening to him at all. That is the way the hon. member for Carleton would have us obey the behest of the hon. member for Edmonton-to comply in every case with the judgment of the British Government.
That is the interpretation which you put upon my words.
We had better read the words. What was the date of my hon. friend's speech?
February 2, I think.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman could give me the page?
I do not remember making any such statement. You will find it on page 445.

Yes, here it is:
About the possibility of converting the Boss factory inside of two years in order to make rifles of a new type. He-
That is, the Prime Minister.

*-lias given us a statement by some official in England who has some doubts about our ability to convert this factory in two years.
Then further on, he says:
I think that that man, whoever he may be, is incompetent.
That is not a fair reading. Go back four or five lines.
Is there any high treason about that?

I did not say that it was high treason. The hon. gentleman said that he did not use the words; I have given not only the words, but his reasons for using them, and all I have to say is that his reasons were just as weak as his assertions.
Either we are bound by the contract or we are not. If hon. gentleman opposite can procure our release from it, we will release the other party to the contract any time at all. If hon. gentlemen opposite can procure the abandonment of the rights of the contractor by one jot or tittle, we will welcome anything whatever, but in the meantime-

Parliament has given
the Government authority to do that, under the War Measures Act.

The hon. member for
St. John City would like to come to the rescue of those people who attacked me for making the simple assertion that we were bound by the contract. He has said that he would not suggest that we were not bound by it; let me, therefore, deal with those who castigate me for saying that we are.

What seems to me to be extraordinary is that my hon. friend tonight has set up a plea by way of confession of the negligence of himself and his friends, but he avoids the point by saying 
that there is a contract here which bound them, lhat is the whole object my hon. friend had in view.
What I say is that the contract binds both parties.
But when the war broke out Parliament gave to this Government the authority to take any step of any kind or description which it might think necessary for the more efficient carrying on of the war.
Haven't I repeated that over and over again.
Then what is the use of repeating that argument tfiat the Government was bound?
The fact that we have power to break a contract does not say that we were not bound by it. The Government might break any contract; we did not need any War Measures Act for that.
That is what Parliament gave the power for.

We might break it under penalty of damages as any individual can do. But I repeat that if we were not bound by this contract, no person, no Government, no individual, no company was ever bound by any contract in the history of the world.
Will the minister allow me to ask him a question? I am following the hon. gentleman very closely.
Will the hon. gentleman wait until I am through?
I caught you too badly before.
Then catch me again.
Does the minister say that the existence of a contract such as this would justify the Government in continuing to accept inefficient arms?
I told the hon. gentleman twenty times that it never would, and we never would have felt we should continue an inefficient arm or any arm if we could get a better one.

Then why talk about
the existence of the contract at all?

Because the hon. gentleman sitting beside my hon. friend challenged me to do so, and dared me to substantiate the statements I made - in Mon-

treal. That is none too strong and none too sound a reason, but it is the only reason I have; it is because I am challenged to do so by hon. gentlemen opposite who do not know any better. We would not have been justified in continuing the manufacture of this or any other rifle had we been able in sufficient time to get a rifle that we knew on sufficient authority was a better rifle to use. That is surely sufficient for the hon. member for St. John. Were we in a position to produce another rifle? Was a year's notice necessary? "Oh," he says, "they never would have taken all that time." I have shown that they took twenty-three months in 1910 and 1911. Was a year's notice necessary? If it was not, what is the plight of hon. gentlemen opposite? If a year's notice was not necessary why did hon. gentlemen opposite provide for a year's notice and put it in the power of the contractor to exact it? If it was not neces'-sary, why did the hon. gentlemen give the contractor power to exact this notice if less time was sufficient? There is no answer- and there cannot be an answer.
The British Government tell us that in theiT judgment two year's time is necessary. " Oh," say some hon. gentlemen opposite, " the British Government have told you that they will supply you with jigs, tools and gauges," .and on that they argue that very little time would be required. Do they not observe that in the very letters, in which the British Government advises that two years would be necessary, they offer to supply these jigs, tools >and gauges? In the same letter in which the British Government offer to give jigs, tools and gauges they offer plans and drawings, etc., and they warn us that we cannot expect substantial deliveries under two years. They may be right or they may be wrong.

After receiving that letter, did the Government or any official go to Sir Charles Ross or any other member of his company and ask them in what time they wpuld 'be willing or able to produce the Lee-Enfield rifle?
Sir Charles Ross often said he could do it in less than a year. We did not ask him, he kept telling us.
Did you go to him?

He came to us. But will any hon. gentleman, on his responsibility as a member, say that we should have taken the unsupported word of a contractor who himself is to make the goods, and who is anxious for an order, and honestly so, that we should take that and have no regard whatever to other authorities even the authority of the British Government?
But did you ever go to Sir Charles Ross and ask him hpw long, in his judgment, it would take to convert his plant to manufacture Lee-Enfield rifles, 10,000 or 20,000, or any quantity?
I have said that Sir Charles Ross told us without our going to him:
In what time, and what did he say?
My recollection is that he stated seven or eight months.

That is when he
was supplied with the jigs and gauges.
Yes, that is my recollection of his conversation. -

That is when he was
supplied with the equipment?

Suppose he said two months, and suppose he was honest in his statement-and I have no reason to question his bona fi'des. Who is the hon. gentleman who will say that we should have no regard for the opinion of the British Government in this matter, especially when th-ur opinion is hacked by their practice 'in Great Britain in this very hour? They know in Great Britain, iat least they have expressed the opinion, that the Enfield .276 is an improvement on the Lee-Enfield which they themselves are producing and using. But they do not change their factories, they do not re-equip their factories to produce the better rifle. Why? Because they know that time, and a long time, would be taken, and that time is the lives of soldiers and that there is no time to spare. That is why they do not re-equip, and that is why they advise us: " Re-equip if you will, but be sure and consider that time will be lost." And we, in our determination of what to do, have regard not only to the judgment of Sir Charles Ross, hut to the judgment of the British Government, hacked up by the practice of the British Government itself. That is our position in relation to that question.
Would the hon. gentleman say just whi.t the decision of this Government has been in regard to this Ross rifle?

The Government, in this question, has reached precisely the point clearly defined by the Prime Minister.

The Government has not decided what order to give or whether any order should! be given.
Mr. MARCH.: They have decided to let the Ross factory continue to operate in Quebec?

They have decided that it shall be re-equipped and adjusted to produce the Enfield .276, and notice has been given accordingly. That notice was given on the first day it was possible to do so, that is on the first day when it was possible to secure a standard sample certified by the inspector of small arais in Great Britain.

Has it also given an
order for any rifles?

I said it has not. We have not yet received the drawings and specifications essential before any further progress on our part can be made. Ever since we received the report and decision of Sir Douglas Haig, we have made every endeavour to put ourselves in a position to make progress, and we have made the fastest progress in our power.
Now then, after the French report, what next occurred? The next thing that occurred was that on the 12th day of May, 1916, a communication was sent, I think it was directed to the ex-Minister of Militia, by Sir Max Aitken, to the effect that a serious situation existed with regard to the Ross lifle, and Sir Max Aitken asked him to show that cablegram to the Prime Min ister. The ex-Minister did as requested, liiat was on the 12th of May.
Did the Prime Minister not also ask the British officers, I think Sir Douglas Haig, for a comparative test?

That is true. Practically the same cablegram that was sent placing it in the hands of Sir Douglas Haig was sent, I think, to Sir Wm. Robertson, and that cablegram asked that after tests under war conditions had been made, the question as to what rifle should be used should be decided by Sir Douglas Haig, and stated that by his decision, whatever it was, we would abide. If the test had (been made, well and good. Sir Douglas Haig took the position on 28th May, 1916, that in his judgment the tests already made were sufficient, and by a letter of that date he advised not us, but the War Office in London, that in his judgment it would be better to arm the troops of Canada with the Lee-Enfleld rifle. That was done in a letter of the 28th May, and it was confirmed in another letter of the 21st June. As a result, the War Office in London by ia communication of the 3rd July following sent to Si.r George Perley who transmitted it to us, expressed the opinion that Sir Douglas Haig's action had been correct, that having been given authority, he had taken it and had .asked our troops be armed with the Lee-Enfleld rifle, and that the Small Arms Committe confirmed that decision.. From that time on, we were in accord; the two Governments and the commander in chief of the forces were in accord that the troops of Canada should toe armed with the Lee-Emfield rifle.

There is just one point that I desire to impress upon the House, and that is that the Prime Minister asked that a competitive test between the two rifles should be made under war conditions; he asked that the best possible test should be made. There was no competitive
test, and there never has been a competitive test made officially by the British Government of these two rifles. I am merely emphasizing my own position. There has been no competitive test. The test referred to by Sir Douglas Haig was a test in which there was no competition at all. The point I am trying to bring out is that a competitive test was not carried out. If it had been, the Ross rifle would have come out ahead.

That correspondence
reached this Government some time in July. I do not remember the exact date. The decision of Sir Douglas Haig was put into effect, he being of the opinion that the tests, *whatever (they had been, were sufficient. He being of that opinion, armed the troops of Canada with the Lee-Enfleld rifle, and thereafter the Ross rifle was not used except, I believe, for special purposes at the front. It must be noted that even at that time Sir Douglas Haig stated that the situation in regard to the Third Division did not apply to the Second Division; in other words, that the complaints which had come from the Third Division had not come from the Second; but his judgment having been made supreme by the action of this Government he decided it was better *all things considered., to adopt the Lee-Ein-fleld. It was adopted then and there, and adopted with our authority. There was no earlier time when we could possibly justify the abandonment of our rifle than the date of the letter of the War Office to Sir George Perley, transmitted to us, and now, I am quite certain, on the table of the House, stating that the situation had changed, and that they, the War Office of Great Britain, assumed the responsibility from that date on of providing the troops of Canada with Lee-Enfields. Until that time they had not undertaken to do so. They had advised us before that that they would not be able to do so, hut the situation had improved in the meantime, and they stated that they were able to do so in July. That being the judgment of Sir Douglas Haig, this Government acquiesced. Indeed, we were the first of the two Governments to say that if Sir Douglas Haig was of opinion that the Lee-Enfleld was better for our troops under all the circumstances, the Lee-Enfleld they should have.
From that time on, the situation, as it confronted the Government of Canada, was altered. Up to that time it was not a *question of the commercial advantage to 'this country at all. It was a question of get-

ting the -best weapon we could put our hands on for the use of our troops at the front. From that time on, namely, from July, when we were advised that the British Government were able to take care of the arming of the Canadian troops with Lee-Enfield rifles, the situation ceased to have the serious aspect it had previously assumed, and it never has assumed the same aspect since. From that time on, it was practically a commercial question, and nothing else. We wanted to produce our rifles, all the rifles we could produce, not because our troops, would otherwise be unarmed but because it was part of the policy of this country to make in this country as much as possible of what this, country used.
In this connection I desire to refer to a speech of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy). In the remarks which he addressed to the House on 29th January last, he used the following words:
No til with.standing' General Haig's statement of the urgency of the case and its approval by the Army Council, which offered to supply Eee-Enflelds, and which requested that no more Ross rifles be brought to England, it was not until August 30, 1916, more than thirteen months after General French's report and sixteen months after the failure of the rifle had been demonstrated at the battle of St. Julien, that the Government of Canada finally gave its consent to the British War Office supplying Lee-Enfields to the second and third Canadian divisions, and expressed the hope that no rearming had been done without their knowledge.
Now I have quoted correctly from the speech of the hon. member; that not until August 30, 1916, did the 'Government of Canada give its consent to the British War Office arming our troops with the Lee-Enfield, and that even then we expressed the hope that it had not been done without our approval. Does the hon. gentleman think that that was quite fair? Does he think it was a correct-I will not use a stronger term-way of stating the contents of the telegram of August 30, 1916? This Government authorized the change on the 15th of May 1916, in a cablegram to Sir Douglas Haig, providing be thought the charge wias in the best interest of our troops. We -authorized it then and no further approval was necessary. We authorized it to he done -and it -was done. A month before the 30th of August our troops were armed with the Lee-Enfields.
Where does that appear?
In the cablegram of the Prime Minister stating we would abide by the judgment of Sir Douglas Haig.
It is not in Hansard.
I think it is right in the file. The cablegram was to Mr. Bonar Law. Secretary of State for the Colonies and it was forwarded at once to the General Officer Commanding at the front.

The hon. gentleman says the cable was sent on the 15th of May. That was a cablegram to Sir Max Aitken. I should like to know the position Sir Max Aitken occupied in relation to this Government and the British Government.
He was appointed by Order in Council, general representative for Canada at the front, and he fulfilled his duties perfectly.
I thought he was an Intelligence Officer, an eye-witness.

The Cablegram was sent to Sir Douglas Haig through the instrumentality of Sir Max Aitken. Sir Max Aitken had conveyed the other information to us, and 'as a 'consequence this cable went back through the same channel. It is in effect a cable to Sir Douglas Haig, and is supplemented by another cablegram on June 5, in which, practically word for word, the same Information was placed before Sir William Robertson, Chief of the Imperial Staff in Great Britain. So that our authority, if Sir Douglas Haig thought it best, -was given on the 15th of May, 1916, and could have been given no sooner.
What was the cablegram of August 30, to which the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) referred as being the first approval on the part of the Government of Canada of the change to the Lee-Enfieid? It is a cablegram from the Governor General to the Colonial Secretary, as follows:-
In pursuance of your cable message of July 11, my advisers announced that Canadian troops at front would in future be armed with Lee-Enfleld rifles.
That is, we announced, in pursuance of the cable of July 11, that our troops would be so armed. The cable continues:-
They are confident that no departure from this decision has been made without their knowledge, but they desire to he informed as to report which has reached them that Fourth Canadian Division was armed with Ross rifles when recently despatched to France.
Now, hon. gentlemen have the cablegram in which we stated that on the authority of the cablegram from the British Government we had long ago announced that our troops hereafter would be armed with Lee-Enfield,.

and we say that notwithstanding that, we have heard a report- that the Fonrth Division have been sent to the front anned with Ross rifles, and we want to know if that has been done without our approval. And the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) tells this House that this was the first time we had approved of our troops being armed with the Lee-Enfield-the very opposite of the cable.
Is there a cablegram on the file dated May 15? I do not find it in Hansard.	.

I was talking of the cablegram of August 30. The cablegram of the 15th of May was from the Prime Minister to Sir Max Aitken, for transmission to Sir Douglas Haig. Thlat is the situation. From that day we have made every endeavour to procure the rifle -and the drawings and -specifications. First of all, we had to procure from the British Government a statement as to what rifle in their judgment would be the rifle 'to be used after the war, what rifle it was best that we should make, having regard to the future. We got that information, and as soon as we got it we immediately proceeded to put ourselves in a position to serve notice on the Ross Rifle Company to -adjust their factory to make the rifle -so recommended, -and we have not lost a day or an hour -since. We have pressed the British Government insistently. No doubt they have done their best under the circumstances, but notwithstanding our pressure it was not until the 20th of January this year that we were in a position to serve notice on the company, because we had not the standard arm which was to accompany the notice according to the contract, and without which the notice would have been practically of no effect at all, and almost worthless to the contractor.
Was that standard arm made in Great Britain or in the United States?

In the United States,
I understand; the British Government is not making it for the reason that they would not take the risk of the delay involved in readjusting their factories to turn out the new rifle.
Mr. PUGStEY:	If the Lee-Enfield in
regard to which notice was given to the Ross Company on- the 20th of January was made in the United States and supplied to the British army, why was there such a long delay in getting one of the standard riflee to the company?

For the reason set out in Mr. Bon-ar Law's cablegram of September 11, 1916. We set out to get that standard rifle in the United States in order to save -time. A report that we were doing so reached the War Office, and on September 11 they cabled this Government asking us not to use a rifle procured in the United States as a standard until it had been inspected by the chief inspector of aims and ammunition of the British Government, and received his imprimatur and approval. Were we right in that or not? Should we have defied them and taken the rifle from the United States as a standard?
When were the contracts let in the United States?

I have a pretty good
idea but do not know that I am justified in giving the dates ot deliveries, but I think I am justified in going this far, that if hon. gentlemen will make inquiry as to the date the contract was given in the United States and note the quantities delivered up to the present hour, I do not think they will find very much support for their optimism in thinking you can re-equip a factory and make a new kind of rifle in a very few months. I do not need to go back and repeat that we do not hide behind the contract. We are not attempting to conceal anything. We are quite free to say that if we could have done better by breaking the contract, we -should have broken it. But we saw nothing better that could be done.
The very last people who should criticise us for not breaking the contract are the men who made the contract themselves. The -criticism comes very ill from those very men who now stand up and make themselves the -complainants. They themselves fathered the contract; they fathered this rifle. They forged the chain? and fastened them on this country, and now they stand up and declaim against us because we did not burst the fetters with which they in itheir folly had bound themselves and all Governments to come.
That is the position in which we stand with respect to this rifle. We have nothing to conceal as regards our conduct, nor as regards our treatment of the whole rifle subject. It is a vital subject; it is a subject that goes to the very heart of our success. We have nothing to conceal; we invite no controversy, but we run away from none. Our course has been clear and is not only defensible, but impregnable from beginning to end. Because it is a vital question, one

of the most important of tthe thousand problems that confront us from day to day, it has received-, in a special degree, the supervision of the Prime Minister, a supervision that has directed iand surveyed, with ceaseless vigilance -and with a care -and an energy that almost passes comprehension, every phase of this work of this Government. On the record of this Government we stand and we fear the criticism of no man. Fortunately for us every step in the path that we have followed is now marked out by a long line of official reconds. They are there for all Canadians to read, and we urge upon the people of Canada to read those records in full and to study them carefully, and we appeal with the -almost confidence to the judgment of every impartial and intelligent man.

Mr. Chairman, as the hon. minister says: We are dealing with one of the most important *phases of our responsibility in connection with the war. We cannot give this matter too careful attention. We are here to listen to the best that the Government can state on behalf of its course in this connection We have listened carefully and we have heard from the lips of the Prime Minister and from the lips of his Solicitor General, whom we all agree is not the least able member of the Cabinet, the best reasons they have to give for the fact that to-day we 'are called upon to vote $2,660,000 for rifles that are not to be used at the battle front. After we have paid to the amount of $6,500,000 for Ross rifles made in Canada, not one battalion, not one platoon of Canadian troops at the front is armed with that rifle, after two and a half years of war. In the face of such facts as these, I ask hon. gentleman on the other side of the House: Of what avail is the special pleading of the Solicitor General here to-night? What difference does it make to this country what advice I have given to the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House 'during this debate, or what advice the hon. member for Pi^m. or any other member has given? The question before the country is not what advice we have given; the question is: What has the Government done and how far can the Government justify what it has done before the high court of public opinion? The question of the furnishing of our troops with what is called small arms, with rifles, is the most important question with which we have to deal; but we are dealing to-day with a vote of $500,000,000, appropriated in bulk for expenditure by this Government for the support of Canada's part in
 .
the war, and on the most vital point in all this vast expenditure, we find the result that I have already stated, that we have spent $6,500,000 and we practically have not a rifle in the firing line, and we are being called upon to-night to vote, if my hon. friend presses his motion, to pay $2,660,000 for rifles that are not yet manufactured and that will never see the front after they are manufactured. This is a far reaching matter. If such is the record of the Government on this the most important feature connected with the war so far as we are concerned, what are we to believe in regard to the other phases which involve the whole of this stupendous expenditure? WTe and our children's children will be paying on account of the burden that we are laying upon the people of the country by this vote to-day. We vote the money freely; our people pay it willingly; but surely we ought to know from the Government that the money is being expended wisely and for the purpose for which it is voted, and yet on this vote for rifles to arm our men we are paying $6,500,000 and we have not a rifle in the firing line.
The Solicitor General, in justification of that position, says that The members on this side of the House, the late Government, fourteen years ago, entered into a contract to make rifles in Canada for the use of Canada, which contract binds Canada for all time, and that because of that contract, this condition that I have spoken of exists and we who have ceased to have direction of the affairs of our country for more than five years are to be held responsible, and these gentlemen who have had full dirrC-tion of the affairs of our country for more than five years are absolutely absolved from responsibility by the special pleading of the Solicitor General and even by the remarks of the Prime Minister the other night. There never was an occasion on which a more absurd contention was presented for the consideration of any deliberative body in the world. While I think it is a waste of time to discuss before this House and the country the respective responsibility of ourselves on this side and they on that side, yet seeing that my hon. friend is a very eminent member of the Government as well as of the legal profession, and that he has laid great stress upon that point and alluded particularly to my humble self, I shall not be accused of trespassing unduly upon the time of the House if I deal with that matter for just one instant. We admit that the Liberal Government made a contract with the Ross Rifle Company; we believe

that it was provident to make such a contract at the time at which it was made, and we believe that it was a provident contract. My hon. friend ha3 said and repeated and repeated that we who made the contract are responsible if the rifles made under that contract are ineffiicient rifles. That contract provides, as I have already said: First, that in case of war or emergency the Government does not need to take rifles from the Ross Rifle Company beyond the number that the Ross Rifle Company can supply to the Government's order. Therefore, the Government was not bound for all time, nor for all rifles. And when the Solicitor General says specifically to a listening world that the Government and country were bound, may I be permitted, Mr. Chairman, with your consent, to suggest that the Solicitor General is attempting to deceive the public.
Oh, oh.

I will just complete that. The second point is, that the contract entered into by the Liberal Government provided that the Ross Rifle Company should make any alterations in the rifle, or the type of rifle, made by them, at the demand of the Government. Therefore, if the pattern of rifle made under the orders of the late Liberal Government was in any degree insufficient, there was within the four corners of the contract-that, I understand, is the expression used by a legal gentleman-specific provision which places the responsibility upon this Government to maintain that rifle in its condition of efficiency. There was a further provision in the contract that if and when the Government desired to have the company make another kind of rifle altogether the company was bound to comply. These gentlemen have been in power for more than five and a half years. It was their responsibility during that period to see to it that the rifles manufactured for this country were efficient; it was within their power during the whole of that time to ensure that they should be efficient according to their viewsN If to-day we have not a battalion, a company, a platoon, at the front armed with Ross rifles, the responsibility is absolutely theirs, and no amount of special pleading, either by the Solicitor General or by the Prime Minister, can place responsibility upon the late Government or upon 'any member on this side of the House. My hon. friend was strong on the point that the rifle which was in the hands1 of the troops who crossed the ocean in September, 1914, was of a pattern which had
been approved by the late Government. Admit for the sake of the argument that this is true. Specify, if you please, that we eliminate the time intervening between the outgo of the Liberal Government and the declaration of war. Assume that there was no provision in the contract which placed the responsibility upon this Government, and say that the late Government was responsible for the type of Mark III Ross rifle. Yet the late Government never ordered a Mark III rifle to be made, and there was never a Mark III Ross rifle made while the late Government was in office. The Solicitor General himself told us to-night that it was not until December, 1912, a year and two months after the late Government had left office, that the first Ross rifle Mark III was delivered.
It was in November.

The hon. gentleman said December, but I will alter it to November if he pleases. Now, I submit that the Government which found no difficulty, no impediment to the cancelling of a contract for the building of a Canadian navy, a contract which they had in their desks when they took office, accompanied by a deposit of $100,000 of securities for its fulfilment, is not in a position to claim that, because the late Liberal Government had sanctioned Mark III Ross rifle, they were not bound to order the making of that rifle, nor to accept delivery of it when it was made. As a matter of fact, the order for the making of Mark III Ross rifle was given by the ex-Minister of Militia (Sir Sam Hughes) and not by a member of the Liberal Government. So, if my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) did not catch what I said a few minutes ago, perhaps he will understand it when I now repeat it: When he made the statement he did attempting to throw responsibility upon the late Government for making an inefficient rifle under the control of this Government, he was attempting to mislead and deceive the public as to the facts of the case.
Nobody believes that, not even the hon. gentleman himself; he has more intelligence than that.

I accept my hon. friend's interruption, considering the source from which it comes. Now, my hon. friend has rested his case on the two points, of responsibility of the late Government, and the assertion that the report of Sir John French did not condemn the Ross rifle. Before I touch these points, let me say, as I said

the other night, that the responsibility for ensuring that the troops of Canada were efficiently armed and equipped rested upon this Government and not upon the Government of Great Britain, upon our military department, and not the military department of Great Britain; and our friends have no right, either in constitutional practice or as a matter of right, to attempt to shelter themselves behind the officers of the British military administration. We maintain a Militia Department for the purpose of ensuring efficiency in the conduct of our military affairs. We cannot call Sir John French before the bar of Canadian public opinion to condemn him for what he says or does. A system of responsible government is supposed to prevail in this country, and we look to the Minister of Militia and to the Prime Minister of our Government to see that efficiency is maintained. My hon. friend attempted to be funny over the idea that I had used a contradiction of argument in speaking of the necessity of our making our equipment conform with the British requirement, and at the same time holding the Government here responsible for inefficiency in the equipment. I can see no contradiction in those arguments; on the contrary, it appears to me that they are in entire and proper sequence. I leave the question as to the merits of that to the judgment of the committee and of the public. I say, therefore, that this Government had no right to wait until Sir John French reported as he did with regard to the Boss rifle. They had a right to inform themselves- it was their first duty on behalf of the people of Canada and of the soldiers of Canada-in regard to the efficiency of that weapon upon which the lives of our soldiers, prestige of our country and the success of the Allied arms depended. They did not do it-that is confessed and admitted; there is no argument about it. Not only did the Government not attempt to inform themselves as to the efficiency of the Boss rifle, but the ex-Minister of Militia has assured us on the floor of the House that the rifle was and is absolutely efficient. It would be absurd to suggest, in view of the attitude of the ex-minister in regard to the rifle, that the Government used due diligence; that the Government was not guilty of absolute negligence concerning the efficiency of this weapon. They are all the more guilty in the matter because amongst their own followers were men who for years had persistently criticised that weapon as manufactured under Liberal administra-
tion. Those critics were either satisfied that a different and superior rifle was in the hands of the troops, or they were willing to submit their criticisms and opinions to political exigency. I do not wish to accuse hon. gentleman on the other side, or indeed, any good citizen of Canada, of being willing to submit such a question as that, involving the issues that it did, to political exigency. I bqlieve that they believed that our troops were armed with an efficient rifle. They had a right to believe that, and today when it is proved that our troops were not armed with an efficient rifle they have a right to hold the ex-minister of Militia and the members of the Government absolutely responsible for the consequences that resulted, terrible though those consequences were.
My bon. friend rests his whole case on the assertion that 'Sir John French reported in favour of the efficiency of the Boss rifle. On my reading of the report, the hon. gentleman's assertion-his argument, his special pleading-has absolutely no foundation; the report of Sir John French can be read only as a condemnation of the Boss rifle as an efficient weapon in the field, based on the experiences of Sir John French in connection with the operations that were under his direction and control, and for which he was responsible. We judge of what a man thinks by what he does, and the higher and more responsible his position, the more that holds true. When Sir John French, without reference to the Canadian Government or to our Militia Department, Lee-Enfields being as scare as the Prime Minister and the Solicitor-General have said they were, disarmed the First Canadian Division of their Boss rifles and re-armed them with Lee-Enfields-^doing so, as he specifically says here, (because he did not wish to send them into a certain important battle armed with the Boss rifle-I say that if lie had covered a. hundred pages with apologies for or explanations of the Boss rifles it would not alter the reasonable and proper conclusion which may be drawn from what he actually did, and the reasons why he did it. My hon. friend reads certain sentences from Sir John French's report (and he ascribes to them certain interpretations that, in my humble judgment, with all due respect, I do not consider that the language permits. In his report to the War Office in London on June 19, 1915, Sir John French, speaking of the committee of investigation, said:
The proceedings of this committee were laid before me on the eve of a serious offensive

operation in which the Canadian division was to take part, and I was at the same time informed that over 3,000, or more than one-third of the infantry, of this division had already succeeded in re-arming themselves with the Lee-Enfleld rifle without any authority having been given for them "to do so.
(1)	To the unanimous opinion of my committee that the Ross rifle could not be relied upon to work smoothly and efficiently in rapid fire with any ammunition other than that of Canadian manufacture;
(2)	to the fact that no ammunition of this nature was available in this country, and that sufficient supplies could not be obtained from England.
Further on he said:
I did not feel justified in sending this division into battle with the Ross rifle, and ord'ered the re-arming of the infantry of the division with the Lee-Enfield rifle, which was carried out before they went into action on the 15th inst.
I submit that there is only one conclusion to be drawn-.from those words; and yet by picking other sentences out of the report, sentences which are not governing in their character, sentences which I am bound to suppose were put there for the purpose of letting down easily the Canadian Department of Militia, the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General have endeavoured to create the impression that Sir John French did not report against the Ross rifle. Sir John French quotes the report of the committee of which he speaks. In his first report he says, in section 7:
I have expressed and acted upon my opinion that, so far as I could test, the ammunition of British manufacture is not suitable for use with Ross rifles, that there is a large and growing feeling of want of confidence in their rifles on the part of the men in the Canadian division, which is amply justified by the report of the committee.
Now, that is a report on the rifle, and that is what Sir John French says. I submit that when the Solicitor General undertook to read another meaning into that report, he was not fair to the House or to the country.
I read the report.

Carefully edited. I will
take the liberty of calling the attention of the House again to some portions of this report of the committee:	[DOT]
Opinion of committee: A unanimous opinion was expressed that Canadian manufactured D.A.C. 1914 Mk. VII ammunition only, of those tried, was suitable for rapid Are with the Ross rifle.
That deals with the question of ammunition, and it points otlt that.only a certain
brand of Canadian ammunition would work satisfactorily in the Ross rifle. He says:
That provided a sufficient supply of Canadian manufactured ammunition of this type could be supplied.
But he did not suggest that it could be provided, it had not been provided, and there was no reason to believe that it would be provided.
The hon. gentleman forgets that the War Office stated at the very same time in reply to that letter that it was provided.

This is the report of the
committee on which Sir John French based his report. I am reading it to the House. It was upon Sir John French'e report that my hon. friend tried to justify himself, it was not on some other report of some body else, it was on this report; and this report explicitly says that the Ross rifle did not work satisfactorily except with a certain kind of ammunition which was not available in sufficient supply.
Read it, it was with re spect to the future.

He stated:
That provided a sufficient supply of Canadian-manufactured ammunition of this type could be supplied.
Provided it could be supplied, but it had not been supplied and Sir John French gave no indication of hie expectation that it could or would be supplied.
The War Office did it.

That is another story.
This is the report which my friend was taking up and upon which he rested his whole case. He edited it carefully and I am giving it exactly as it is. He says, and I would like the committee to listen to this feature very carefully:
The other defects apparent were not sufficient to condemn the Ross rifle in view of the present shortage of rifles generally.
They were sufficient to condemn the Ross rifle if other rifles had been available. Is that the proper meaning of these words? There is no other meaning that can be attached to them, and if that is not a straight and square condemnation of the Ross rifle on its merits, then the English language has lost its significance at the hands of my hon. friend. It goes on:
The committee were practically unanimous in advising that the Ross rifle should be employed on the lines of communication, and



that if possible, the Canadian troops should be armed with the British rifle.
The merry jest of the right hon. the Prime Minister the other night that the Ross was a rifle for peace and not for war, under the Liberal make, is borne out by this report of the committee that it was good for some places where fighting was not expected, on the lines of communication, but that the troops should be armed with the British rifle. Does my hon. friend attempt to justify the action of this Government in asking this House to vote $2,-
660,000	to make 80,000 more of these rifles that were specifically condemned in these ternis by the authority to which he deferred as being absolute in this matter? The committee sat on the 5th June, 1915, and the report of Sir John French was made on the 19th of June. You will observe that the difficulties and delays which have interfered with the action of this Government in dealing with this matter of rifles did not interfere with Sir John French forwarding his report in a very short time after he got the opinion of the committee to investigate the rifle. There was no delay on the other side of the water; there has been nothing but delay on this side of the water.
Just to go into some of the details of this report, 1 will ask any man who cares to bring his judgment to bear what conclusion he could possibly reach other than that reached by the committee and transmitted by Sir John French to the War Office.
With regard' to the following specific points which the committee was asked to answer, the questions and answers are as stated below:
1.	There are frequent reports that the bolt action jams after about 5 rounds.
Now that is not a question of ammunition, that is & question of construction and mechanism, and that is the first statement that the committee made, " there are frequent complaints that the bolt actipn jams after about 5 rounds," and the Solicitor General tells this House and this country that the report of Sir John French justifies the Government in refusing to take action to replace the Ross rifle with a m.ore efficient weapon as they should have done, and could have done under the contract. The committee go on to say:
2.	Full value of rapid fire cannot be developed unless:
(a)	Ammunition of Canadian manufacture
is used.
(b)	Rifle is perfectly clean.
It will be observed in this No. 2, the question of ammunition is considered, and

it is stated that the rifle is better adapted for use with ammunition of Canadian manufacture than that of British manufacture. That has nothing whatever to do with the first clause, which said that the bolt action jams after about 5 rounds.
Why did it not jam when they fired 100 rounds in the trial?
I do not know.
You had better read it.
Does my hon. friend know??
Yes, it was because they were using Canadian ammunition. They fired 100 rounds and it did not jam.
That is not what this report says, and I can only give what the report says.
It is exactly what it says.

This is what my hon. friend the Solicitor General rested his case on, and I am willing to rest my case upon it also. I ask the House to read that section, and to take it as it stands, and as it was meant to stand. The second part of section 2 is that the rifle must be perfectly clean. That is a 'condition that cannot be maintained in trench warfare, and the rifle whose efficiency depends upon perfect cleanliness is net an efficient weapon in trench warfare such as prevails to-day. That has been the contention all the time. It was reported from the front by the first men who went there, and it is borne out by this statement by this committee. The report goes on to deal with the question of ammunition:- -
That English-made ammunition is slightly larger than Canadian so that immediately the cartridge exploded the cartridge case fills the chamber so tightly as to cause a jam.
That is not in place of the other disabilities ; that is in addition to the other disabilities. No. 4 reads:-
That orders exist that on no account are troops to take out their magazine as it necessitates stripping the rifle.
That is the objection. Then:-
(b) Unless the magazine is unloaded every 24 hours and the spring action eased, the magazine fails to respond.
That had nothing to do with the ammunition.
(5) That dirt accumulates easily in the holt head and also in the receptive thread in the breech of the rifle. Owing to difficulty of cleaning jams are caused.
That has nothing to do with ammunition:

(6) The screw of the bolt expands under heat and renders it difficult to open the breech (presumably due to the number of bearing surfaces affected.
That is to say, under rapid fire the bolt heats and causes jams.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know that my hon. friend does not desire to mislead the committee, hut what he is doing is this: he is reading the questions iae if they were answers, while the answers are given below. He hae apparently become greatly confused. The first twelve of these questions raise points which the committee were to investigate, and he is reading them as if they were the reports of the investigators.
Precisely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The reports of the investigators are further down, 1, 2, 3, 4 and up to 12. So let us understand what the situation is, and not run away with the idea that what the hon. gentleman is reading is the report of the committee. What he is reading is matter submitted for the consideration of the committee.
That is absolutely correct, hut the answers themselves do not give an intelligent knowledge of the matter. .

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
If my hon.
friend wants to give an intelligent statement of what the committee did find, he should read the points which he mentions and then read the findings of the committee on them. He has not been doing that.
Mr. OLIVER? T will follow the Prime Minister's suggestion.
(1)	There are frequent reports that the bolt action jams after about 5 rounds.
The answer to that is, "yes."
(2)	Pull value of rapid cannot be developed unless: (a) ammunition of Canadian manufacture is used.
Hear, hear.

The second is:
(b) Rifle is perfectly clean.
The answer to that is:
Pull value of rapid fire can be developed with ammunition of Canadian manufacture only.
(b) This point was not tested.
That is the second.

Yes. The third is-
English-made ammunition, is slightly larger than Canadian.
That is of course the contention in regard to the ammunition. The answer is:
33i
The British-made cartridge case appears to he of a slightly thicker gauge than that of Canadian manufacture and the diameter of the cartridge immediately under the rim appears to be slightly greater than that of Canadian manufactured ammunition. This may be the cause of jamming.
Hear, hear.
But it does not say that it is.
Oh, oh.
This may be a very jocular matter to some hon. members, but the question is asked specifically, and the answer is made by a responsible committee who say it may be. They do not say it is.
What does Sir John French recommend?
That the rifle be taken away.
Not at all; just read his recommendation.
I am going to read it.
He recommended that we enlarge the chamber, and that is just what we did.
He took the rifles away and replaced them with Lee-Enfield rifles; what he argued about is a matter of minor consideration. Remember, what he did, he did on the strength of this report.
Yes.
That was his interpretation of the report.
Until the chamber was enlarged, and we got Canadian ammunition.
Not at all.
Certainly.
Then the hon. member is in this position, if he says that, he says that Sir John French did not know his business.
No, no.

Because, after the chamber had been enlarged, Sir Douglas Haig reported on it exactly as Sir John French had reported. Therefore, either Sir John French did not know his business, or he did not report as my hon. friend suggests he reported.
The report is there.

I am telling him that it is there, and the report is-I will read it again. It says:
There is a large and growing feeling of want of confidence in their rifle on the part of the men in the Canadian division which is amply justified hy the report of the committee.
Can there be any plainer language than that. Then he says:
I did not feel justified In sending this Division into battle with the Ross rifle, and ordered the re-arming of the infantry of the division with the Lee-Enfield rifle, which was carried out before they went into action on the 15th instant.
He gives the reasons; you are afraid to give the reasons.

I am reading the reasons; I am not afraid of them. I say that the reasons are ample. Either they are ample, or Sir John French was not fit for his position. Now, I do not think that either my hon. friend or myself is in a position to criticise Sir John French. The ex-Minister of Militia may do so, but I do not think we are in that position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Or the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell).

Possibly, but when Sir John French on this report takes certain action and says that he takes certain action on this report, I am bound to believe that he did what he did for the reason that he gave, and the reason which was good enough for him ought to have been good enough for this Government.
(4) That orders exist that on no account are troops to take out their magazine as it necessitates stripping the rifle.
The answer to that is: "Yes".
The next is:
4.	(b) Unless the magazine is unloaded every 24 hours and the spring action eased, the magazine fails to respond.
The answer is:
Possibly this is the case, but the committee were unable to test this point.
Next:
5.	That dirt accumulates easily in the bolt head and also in the receptive thread in the breech of the rifle. Owing to difficulty of cleaning jams [DOT] are caused.
The answer is:
This may be so, but the rifles were not tried under dirty conditions.
Next:
6.	The screw of the bolt head expands under heat and renders it difficult to open the breech (presumably due to the number of bearing surfaces affected.)

The answer is:
The expansion of the bolt, head w'as not apparent when firing 100 rounds of Canadian-manufactured ammunition.
Next:
7.	The Ross rifle sight is defective because of its delicacy and the smallness of the figures which make it difficult to adjust the sight easily.
The answer is:
Admittedly the figuring of the sighting Is small and difficult to read as compared to the British Lee-Enfield rifle.
Next:	.
8.	The magazine case is too thin and is dented' easily. This causes a jamb as the spring cannot work.
The answer is:
The magazine case is flat and any dent therein would seriously affect the spring therein.
Next:
9.	The foresight is not good for service work. The circular cover easily gets filled! with mud and is difficult to clean.
The answer is:
The committee did not consider . that any great amount of difference existed in this respect in comparison with the British rifle.
Next:
10.	A hole has recently been bored in the base of the magazine to enable the cleaning of the magazine to be carried out without stripping the rifle.
The answer is:
This hole should be covered by a small revolving plate, adjusted by a screw.
Next:
11.	It is far easier to load the Lee-Enfield rifle than the Ross rifle with a clip of ammunition. A Lee-Enfield rifle takes 10 rounds, a Ross 5 rounds.
The answer is:
Undoubtedly the loading of the Lee-Enfield can be carried out in half the time, mainly owing to the fact that the guide for the clip on the British rifle is directly over the magazine chamber.
Next:
12.	That the shape of the fore part of the chamber of the Ross rifle is different to that of the Lee-Enfield. That this does not allow of the same expansion and is the cause of the jam.
Undoubtedly there is a difference of the shape of the fore part of the chamber, but the committee was not able to decide that this was the cause of the jam.
And this is the representation upon which my hon. friend rests his case, that the Government was justified in enlarging the chamber of the Ross rifle as a means of

preventing jams, instead of ordering a new rifle at that time, as they were entitled to do under the terms of the contract made by the Liberal Government.
Did not Sir John French recommend us to enlarge the chamber?
I am reading the report of the committee appointed by Sir John French.
Why does not the hon. gentleman answer my question? Did not Sir John French recommend us to enlarge the chamber, and not abandon the rifle at all?

I am not discussing what Sir John French said. I am discussing this point: We have been considering the reasons why the rifle jammed, and it has been contended by hon. gentlemen opposite that the rifle jammed because the chamber was too small, or thait Sir John French believed it jammed because the chamber was too small. The Government delayed more than a year from taking measures to secure an efficient rifle under the contract, because of the statement of Sir John French. And here we have a report of the committee appointed by Sir John French, and that report states that the committee were not able to decide that the bore of the chamber was the cause of the jamming.

Why did Sir John
French recommend us to enlarge the chamber? And he having so recommended, will the hon. gentleman say that we should not have followed his recommendation?

In a case where the credit of Canada is at stake, where the lives of our men and the success of bur armies depend upon the efficiency of the rifle, and when Sir John French reports that he disarmed our men of the Ross rifle, as he did, before he dared send them into action-in such a case I would most certainly take what he did before what he said, even if he said what my hon. friend says he said, for if he said it, he said it without the authority of the committee he had himself appointed to report. The report of the committee, I assume, was available to this Government along with Sir John French's report. It was sent by Sir John French with his own report for the information of this Government, and they are responsible for not giving due consideration to the report of this committee, whatever Sir John French saw fit to report.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman contend also that the British Government should have thrown away the Lee-Enfield rifle, instead of enlarging the chamber as they did?

I know nothing about the Lee-Enfield, and have no idea what the British Government ought to do. I am talking for the soldiers of Canada and the people of Canada. That is the business that is under the hand of the Prime Minister, and that is quite sufficient to absorb the attention of the best of us for the present. I do not know what the British Government did, why they did it, or what the result was. But I do know that this Government delayed a full year in ordering an efficient rifle, which they should have ordered and could have ordered under the contract, while they were enlarging the chamber and tempering the bolts; and at the end of that time Sir Douglas Haig found, as Sir John French had found, that the rifle was inefficient, and that the troops had lost confidence in it. As a matter of fact, the slaughter of Canadians, armed with the Ross rifle, under Sir Douglas Haig's command in 1916, was greater than the slaughter under Sir John French's command in 1915.
The same rifle?
Absolutely the same.
And the slaughter was greater?
More men were engaged.
The German slaughter was greater, too.

Possibly; I do not know. I am not seriously concerned about the German slaughter. What I am seriously concerned about is this: When I know that Germany is equipped with the best arm that science can devise and money supply, it is up to the. Government of Canada not to delay or question or haggle, but to make sure that the soldiers of Canada, too, have a weapon as good as science can devise and money supply.
If the hon. gentleman knows that the Germans are armed with the best weapon that science can devise and money supply, why does he recommend this Government to order Lee-Enfields?

My hon. friend is good at conundrums, and I will let him answer that himself; it is really not material. I was desiring to recall some parts of my

hon. friend's suggestions in regard to myself, but they have slipped my memory, so I will not trouble the House with refer-ing to them.
We have spent a great deal of time here in discussing this question of the Ross rifle, and for my part I have no apology to offer for having done so. What has struck me most seriously in this connection is the fact that this Government, charged with this stupendous responsibility, could consent to take up the line of argument and the form of discussion that it has seemed good to them to follow. To the damning conditions that exist they set up the plea of due diligence in the effort to amend those condiitons. There is, to my mind, a most striking resemblance in the attitude of the Government in regard to the making of efficient rifles in Canada to that which prevailed a year or more ago in regard to the making of munitions of other kinds iD Canada, such as shells and fuses and other articles of a like character. Our hon. friends must accept the position that the attitude was taken that Canada could not do this and Canada could not do that, but Canada did do this and Canada did do that in regard to other munitions of war. munitions that had never been manufactured before in Canada, that had never been manufactured before on this side of the Atlantic. We were able to establish factories, to secure capital, to train men, to enter upon forms of industry that we had never before seen or heard tell of almost: but we were not able to secure the skill or the capital or the energy or we were nor able to take the measures that necessity called upon us to take to give our soldiers an efficient weapon with which to meet our enemies in the field of battle. I cannot imagine how any Government can accept such a position as calmly as they have done, and particularly I cannot understand how. in the face of all that has been said, of the fact that they have not been able to make out a case for themselves before the country, they can come before this House and ask us to vote $2,660,000 for the manufacture of still more of these rifles which the British Government practically refuse to allow them to send over to England and which they refuse to allow our armies in France to be armed with further.

Is the hon. gentleman aware that the British Government has ordered 100,000 of these rifles and that it has refused to cancel the order, is still taking

delivery of them and will be for months to come?

I am not concerned about the British Government; but now the hon. gentleman has risen to his seat, he reminds me of that little matter which slipped my mind and sio I shall be able to refer to it. The committee will pardon me if I bring this matter to their attention. The committee will recall that my hon. friend was very strong on the point that the Government of Canada had on the 15th of May ordered the arming of our troops with Lee-Enfleld rifles.
Authorized, if Sir Douglas Haig approved.
What my hon. friend tried to convey to the country was that an order had been issued for the arming of the troops with Lee-Enfleld rifles.
I did not say that.

My hon. friend did not
say that and now he says he does not mean what he said,

What I said meant exactly what I said, exactly what I intended, namely, that we had authorized the change if in the judgment of Sir Douglas Haig it was the best thing to do. That is exactly what I stated and what is true.

On February 2 my hon.
friend the member for Carleton (Mr. Car-veil) read to the House from the papers that were laid upon the Table a cable message from the Governor General to the Secretary of State for the Colonies. The message, which is dated Ottawa, June 5, 1916, is reported on page 410 of the Unrevised Hansard and contains the following:
Secret.
Following from Prime Minister for Sir William Robertson. By reason of rumored dissatisfaction with Ross rifle I held consultation with General Hughes on 15th May and sent unofficial message to Commander in Chief that we were prepared to leave matters to his judgment after making all necessary tests of both rifles under such conditions as are experienced at the front.
Just w'hat I said.

I think my hon. friend
conveyed the 'impression that he had sent an official message, not an unofficial message.
I did not say whether [DOT] it was official or unofficial.

That is precisely the point. My hon. friend did not say that he had

sent an unofficial message. He did not say that he had sent a message that couild be withdrawn under certain circumstances.
It was not withdrawn.
No, it was not withdrawn.
What is the difference, then?

What my hon. friend did was to put before the House what he desired the House and the country to understand, namely, that the Government had taken the responsibility at that date of ordering the troops to be armed with Lee-Enfield rifles.	.
No, I did not.
Now he admits that he did not do so on that date.
Certainly I never said so. I said exactly what you read.
Never meant to say so?
Never meant to say so and never did say so. I said exactly what is stated in that cable message.
No, my hon. friend will have to withdraw a little of that because "unofficial" is stated in this cable message and he did not state "unofficial".
I did not pay a bit of attention to it. Will my hon. friend tell me what difference it makes as long as the message was not withdrawn?
It is not a question as to whether it was withdrawn or not. It was a question of the intent of the message, and the intent is as plain as day.
Without withdrawal, the effect is the same.
This leaves open the privilege of withdrawal.
It was not withdrawn.
It was not an order?
I never said it was an order; I said it was an authorization.
We are quite in agreement. All I wanted was to get the position of the hon. gentleman as it is and not as he desired it to appear to the country.
I desired it to appear just as it is.
Was that the last telegram that was sent in this connection?
No, there was one on 5th of June, one on the 24th of June and several since.
Was there not a reply to this telegram received from Sir Douglas Haig?
Not that I received.

There was a despatch
from Sir Douglas Haig?
He reported to the War Office.
Yes, he reported to the War Office in pursuance of that communication.
I presume so. Perhaps he had another communication from the War Office. I do not know.
I think it is very likely he had, but anyway he reported on the 28th of May, and he reported specifically without equivocation for the re-arming of the Canadian troops with the Lee-Enfield rifle.

We had authorized him to do what he thought best before we got the report. That report was -sent to the War Office and by them it was' transmitted to Sir George Perley and sent out to us in July. Rut the troops had been re-armed already,' and this was done with our authority.

I think the telegram I have reference to is in Hansard, but I cannot put my finger on it at the moment, and I will not delay the committee. As a matter of fact, the Government did not accept the report of Sir Douglas Haig.
Mr. MEIGHEN. He did not report to us, but to the War Office.
This Government sent another despatch which insisted that in their opinion the Ross rifle was an efficient rifle.

We sent on the 24th June, before we had seen Sir Douglas Haig's report, submitting the same proposal to him-that a change should be made if in their judgment it seemed best. And we got that report in July.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may have got confused about a letteT of 31st August, page 425 of Hansard.

On 7th June, the Prime Minister sent a despatch to the War Office, containing the following sentence:
The Ross rifle is the only one we are at present equipped to make in Canada, and we believe it to be efficient if properly handled.

To this Sir Douglas Haig replied on 21st June:
After consultation with the officer in command during recent heavy fighting, the experience of commanding officer in this fighting was that the Canadians of Third Division at least had lost confidence in their rifle. I must therefore adhere to my recommendation that the 2nd and 3rd Canadian Divisions should be re-armed shortly with the short Lee-Enfield rifle, and X would recommend that the necessary steps to give effect thereto be taken without delay.
Sir Douglas Haig bad' reported on 28th May in favour of re-arming the troops with the Lee-EnfieJid rifle. On 7th June this Government reported against that report in the terms that have 'been read.

If the hon. gentleman listened to what I said, or if he goes by the document, he must 'be aware that that statement is n'ot correct. Sir Douglas Haig's report was made on 28th May. I have statedd'hiat it was written to the War Office. This reached us through Sir George Perley in the month of July. We did not protest against the report of Sir Douglas Haig when we did no't get it, of course.

My hon. friend may, perhaps, recall that on 17th May last I had the honour to bring to the attention of the House a certain extract, a letter addressed by General Alderson to General Gwatkin and published in the Ottawa Citizen. The Prime Minister said that before that date he had cabled to Sir Douglas Haig for a Teport on the Ross rifle. I am bound to suppose that the Prime Minister received a reply.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have explained to my hon. friend over and over again that I sent the message through the same channel as that through which I received communication. The telegram came from Sir Max Aitken, on the 13th or 14th, and on the 15th I sent a message to Sir Douglas Haig through the person through whom I had got that message.

Is this the situation? Having received a telegram dated 12th May from Sir Max Aitken to the Minister of Militia of that time, saying that a serious condition had arisen in regard to the Ross rifle, the Prime Minister stated to the House that he had cabled to Sir Douglas Haig, through Sir Max Aitken. And do the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General tell this House and the country that they never heard any more about that matter until July?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: We heard nothing more except what is contained in the correspondence brought down.

I am assuming, for the credit of the Government, that the report of Sir Douglas Haig, made on 28th May, was in response to the cablegram sent by the Prime Minister, as stated. If that is not the case, and if they did not hear from Sir Douglas Haig until July, I can only say that the Government is absolutely condemned for not using'due diligence in securing information as to the condition of the Ross rifle. They had received an urgent and special 'message from their special agent in regard 'to a serious condition on the field of battle, and they still tell this House that they heard no more about it until July? Well, if that is the measure of this Government's sense of its responsibility in regard to a matter so grave as this, we may as well close the discussion. This Government expends tens of thousands of dollars to keep a military staff in Canada and in England, and to maintain communication between them. We can get everything attended to, apparently, except this Ross rifle business. But it is the most important thing that claims our attention. Either that report of Sir Douglas Haig was in response to the cablegram of the Prime Minister, or it was not. Either the Government heard of it, or it did not. If they did not hear it, if they got no response, that means that they did not use due diligence to gain a knowledge of the circumstances to which the despatch of their agent refeis.
What about the cablegram that followed?

If they did receive Sir Douglas Haig's despatch-and I am bound to believe that they did-then they did not accede to the arming of our troops with Lee-Enfleld rifles until they had put in the protest which I have read, until Sir Douglas Haig had made his reply, repeating his first recommendation, and until the War Office had communicated with this Government ordering them, in effect, not to send any more Ross rifles to England.
What is the use of explaining anything to the hon. gentleman if he ignores both the explanation and the facts that are clearly stated in the documents?
My hon. friend will have to take the facts as I give them.
You do not give them.
I give the facts as they are.

You refuse to listen when I tell you about the telegrams that were sent.
Mr. OLIVER; My hon. friend insists that I have not stated the facts. I will give place to him in order to afford him an opportunity of stating the facts as be believes them to be.
I have already done so two or three times, but if the hon. gentleman wants it again, I will give it to him.
Again, please.

I will take from my hon. friend just what he has said, and I ask him what position the Government is in when, having a High Commissioner in London who was a member of the Government, having this special agent there with all the necessary paraphernalia at hand, they could not get an answer to a question as important as this? I say that the Government is absolutely condemned for lacking diligence in dealing with this matter. My hon friend says that on May 15 they gave specific instructions for the re-arming of the troops with Lee-Enfield rifles, subject to Sir Douglas Haig's opinion. On the 7th they again wrote to the War Office saying:
The Ross rifle is the only one we are at present equipped to make in Canada. We believe it to be efficient if properly handled.
They were not leaving it to Sir Douglas Haig.
Oh, yes, we were. Read all of it.
I am reading this part of it, which carries its own meaning.
No, it does not.

The meaning of that paragraph was that this Government desired a report in favour of the Ross rifle-some such report as they got from General French. But they did not get it from Sir Douglas Haig; that is the only difference. They tried to get it, but they were not successful.
What nonsense.

My hon. frienji is to be congratulated on his parliamentary courtesy. The fact remains that we are called upon to vote this money to a Government which, on its own confession, from start to finish, has convicted itself of absolute lack of diligence on the most important subject under its consideration. They have convicted themselves of leaving in the hands of our soldiers an inefficient rifle after they knew it to be inefficient, and when the terms of the contract with the rifle company enabled them to change that inefficiency to efficiency whenever they desired to do so.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The resolution before the committee is to be considered in the same manner as a resolution of Supply. The amendment that the member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has proposed does not seem to be in order, for the following reasons:	The Governor General
having given his consent to the resolution under consideration, it is not competent for this committee to do otherwise than to agree, reduce, negative, supersede or withdraw by leave. May, in the 11th edition, under the heading, "Committees on Exceptional Expenditure," says:
"Procedure in a Committee of the Whole House appointed to consider expenditure not included in the Estimates for the year's supply follows, in principle, the procedure of the Committee of Supply.

Under the heading, "The Committee of Supply," the same author says:
Each resolution for a grant forms a distinct motion, which can only be dealt with by being agreed to, reduced, negatived, superseded, or, by leave, withdrawn.
I could quote Bourinot, who, page 427, expresses the same opinion. A decision of the same nature was given during the last session hy the Chairman, of Committee's and may be found in Hansard of May 15, 1916, page 3944. Therefore, in my judgment, it appears that the amendment is not in order, and I so rule.

I do not question your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but I think that this motion was put to the committee once by the Chairman to-night. Members on the other side cried "Lost" and it was, I am almost sure, declared lost until an hon. gentleman rose to make a few additional observations. I am not quite sure that once a motion has been put to the committee the chairman can very well rule it out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment was not declared lost, but, for the reasons stated, the amendment has been ruled out of order, and so I declare it.

For reasons which have been explained to me by the Prime Minister, I think it wise to allow this resolution to get into the bill stage, with this understanding of course, that no gentleman who wishes to discuss this further in the committee stage of the Bill will be thought to be retarding the passage of the measure. That is not our object at all. Several gentlemen on this side, thinking the discussion would last so late to-night that the resolution would not be passed, went home. They have some observations to make on other ' phases of it, and I should like the Prime Minister to fully understand that in agreeing to the passage of this Resolution it is understood these gentlemen will not be thought to be taking up the time of the House unduly or taking advantage of the situation if they discuss the Bill.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have a great deal of sympathy with the hon. members who have gone home, and I should be the last to desire to restrict them in discussion when we come to Committee on the Bill. Some information has been asked for which I shall be very glad to give when we come to the committee stage of the Bill, and there will be exactly the same opportunity of discussion then that there has been upon the Resolution.
fThe Chairman.]

I should like to say a few words when the Bill gets into committee, more especially with regard to the equipment which was supplied to the Canadian troops and which was discarded when they reached England. I asked a question with regard to the Oliver equipment, but the Minister side-stepped the question by converting it into a motion for a return. I should like to get the information before the Bill reaches the committee stage.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
All of these
political stories about large sums having been lost to the country through equipment having been discarded will toe found to have very little foundation. Information on that subject can be given to my hon. friend. I made some pretty careful inquiries into it, and I shall have the information for my hon. friend.
Resolutions reported, read the first and second time, and agreed to.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 24, for granting to His Majesty aid for military and naval defence.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
On the motion of Sir Robert Borden, the House adjourned at 12.40 a.m. Tuesday.
Tuesday, February 6, 1917.
